Its funders (IDRC, FCDO, MacArthur, Mellon, Kellogg, the 11th Hour Project) are entirely separate from safety money, and some members, DAIR above all, openly oppose the x-risk framing.
sector:indigenous.missing: Nobody translates between this tradition and the safety core with Indigenous consent. As a result, its relational ontology never reaches the problems about the AI itself, and its working consent tools never reach training-data or evaluation pipelines. That is why 0 of 15 are on the classic map and no x-risk funder backs any of them. The discovery pass for this tradition also ran with no web searches, so the potential and bridge rings are under-sampled.

cell_notes.note: Empty, and this is a real opening. It should not be filled by pulling Indigenous groups into the x-risk ecosystem. 'Core' means belonging to the safety community. The plural_world sweep found no Indigenous-led or decolonial group that does, and one check search for an Indigenous-knowledge alignment fellowship found none either. The useful version is a core organisation with Indigenous co-leadership or a standing, protocol-governed partnership (see the fellowship opening), not an adjacent group relabelled as core.

Only one entry, and the thinness is partly real and partly a search gap. Real: old-ways-new is the only entry that uses safety language, and that rests on one person's role (Angie Abdilla as a reviewer of the International AI Safety Report). Search gap: the plural_world angle ran with no web searches. One search for this note turned up two 2026 leads that are not on the map: the Beyond WEIRD online conference (16 Sept 2026, with Jason Edward Lewis and Maui Hudson) and the Relational Futures project on how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples respond to AI, including companions. The coding is also cautious. technecultura (its founder contributed to the International AI Safety Report and sits on the advisory panel of the Global South AI Safety Report) and masakhane (a member of the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI that plans multilingual safety benchmarks) are borderline bridges.

Only two entries (local-contexts and foundation-for-endangered-languages), mostly because of how the search was done, and that hides a real opening. Only minority-language bodies were swept systematically, and none of them (FPCC, First Languages Australia and others) had AI work. Indigenous data-governance and impact-assessment bodies, whose methods carry over directly, were never searched. Examples: the First Nations Information Governance Centre (OCAP principles), Maiam nayri Wingara in Australia, the US Indigenous Data Sovereignty Network, and practitioners of free, prior and informed consent. Some of these may already have AI work; I haven't checked. The one such body that was found, local-contexts, has no AI work at all (transfer none_yet). The methods exist; the bridge to AI does not.

sector:indigenous.key_insight: All 6 Indigenous-led organisations among the map's 715 sit in this tradition, and none is on the aisafety.com map. 14 of its 15 entries are tagged 'rights and plural voices', and none is tagged AI moral status, agency or multi-agent AI. The field reads the tradition only as data rights. Yet its most distinctive contribution, kinship obligations to non-human relations, speaks directly to problems about the AI itself. Abundant Intelligences even runs a multi-agent systems pod, and its own profile says its account bears on AI moral status.

openings.title: Wire Indigenous consent labels into AI training-data pipelines
openings.summary: Tools for collective consent and provenance over data already exist, but nothing connects them to the tools that assemble and audit training corpora: Local Contexts' TK and BC Labels with their Hub API, GIDA's CARE Principles and IEEE 2890-2025, and Te Hiku's Kaitiakitanga Licence. A small technical and governance project could map them onto the preference signals and provenance tools dataset builders already use, then pilot the result on an open corpus.
openings.detail: Local Contexts is coded none_yet: its site has no AI work. Its September 2026 guidance with Creative Commons pairs the Labels with CC licences, but my search found nothing linking them to CC signals or to tools for filtering training data. creative-commons (which runs CC signals) and data-provenance-initiative are both on the map as adjacent and are natural technical partners. Provenance matters for safety as well as rights: knowing what a model absorbed, and on whose terms, is part of assurance and model documentation. Success would look like this: open-corpus builders and at least one lab honour the Labels, including a 'no AI use' state, when filtering; model documentation reports Indigenous data provenance; and AI Safety Institutes ask about it. Risks: the Labels could become consent-washing; communities may prefer outright refusal to machine-readable permissions; the signals cannot be enforced; Local Contexts and GIDA must lead and may decline; and x-risk funders may see the safety link as indirect, so Humanity AI or Mellon (which already funds Local Contexts) are likelier backers.
steps: Fund a scoping workshop led by Local Contexts and GIDA, with Creative Commons and the Data Provenance Initiative, to agree which Label and Notice states map to which machine-readable signals, refusal included.
Build an open-source annotator that reads Local Contexts Hub API and IEEE 2890 metadata and flags or excludes records, then test it on an open pretraining corpus.
Use Old Ways, New's reviewer seat on the International AI Safety Report and Te Mana Raraunga's submission practice to propose a data-provenance line in evaluation and model documentation.
openings.evidence: local-contexts is in the potential ring with transfer none_yet. global-indigenous-data-alliance, te-hiku-media and te-mana-raraunga-m-ori-data-sovereignty-network are all coded 'standards'. 0 of 15 entries are on the classic map. The indigenous × assurance cell holds only one entry (masakhane). angle_notes (c): these governance tools 'appear on no AI-safety map'. One search found no integration of the Labels into AI pipelines.

openings.title: Fellowship pairing Indigenous knowledge holders with AI-welfare and alignment researchers
openings.summary: Indigenous kinship ontologies are among the most fully worked-out accounts of obligations to non-human minds. Yet the map has no entry from this tradition on AI moral status, agency or multi-agent AI. A co-led fellowship on the Princint model would place knowledge holders from Abundant Intelligences and Old Ways, New alongside model-welfare and cooperative-AI researchers, under Indigenous protocols.
openings.detail: Abundant Intelligences runs to February 2029 with 48 co-investigators and a multi-agent systems pod, and has published Guidelines for Indigenous-centred AI Design. Its profile notes it has no ties to the AI-safety community. Possible counterparts are all on the map: eleos-ai-research and anima-labs (AI welfare and relational study of models), softmax (organic alignment), ai-alignment-network (Japanese 'intelligence symbiosis') and principles-of-intelligence, which shows the format travels by hosting its fellowship in Cape Town from November 2026. The Beyond WEIRD conference (16 Sept 2026) shows Indigenous researchers already meeting AI researchers, but without any safety framing. Success would be co-authored work that turns relational obligations into proposals that can be tested and published both in an alignment venue and in an Indigenous-governed one. Examples: welfare-assessment criteria, reciprocity norms for model deprecation, multi-agent conduct norms. Knowledge holders would be paid and outputs would carry TK Labels. Risks: knowledge extracted as 'alignment targets' and stripped of its land and community context, which the 2020 position paper warns against; the x-risk framing repelling partners (as DAIR's TESCREAL critique shows); a very small pool of people; and int/a's own position, since it is not Indigenous-led and should convene rather than direct.
steps: int/a asks Abundant Intelligences and Old Ways, New whether they want a co-designed exchange, and offers to pay for their time to design it before any researcher is recruited.
Fund a two-day closed workshop with Eleos, Anima Labs, Softmax, ALIGN and Princint to settle three or four concrete shared questions.
Run a pilot cohort of four to six pairs, possibly attached to Princint, co-funded by JTF's Future of Intelligence venture and the 11th Hour Project (which already funds Abundant Intelligences).
openings.evidence: The indigenous × ai_status, × agency and × multi_agent cells are empty. Ring counts are core 0 and bridge 1. angle_notes (a): 'A PIBBSS-style fellowship pairing Indigenous knowledge holders with alignment researchers does not exist.' The plural_world key insight: kinship, Ubuntu, kyōsei and Buddhist relational framings are 'not synthesised'. abundant-intelligences carries the full_spectrum badge.

openings.title: Adapt free, prior and informed consent to AI deployments and data centres
openings.summary: Indigenous peoples and extractive industries have decades of practice with free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) and community-led impact assessment. Examples are UNDRIP's FPIC articles, the CBD's Akwé: Kon guidelines, and the Indigenous-knowledge provisions of Canada's 2019 Impact Assessment Act. AI impact assessments, by contrast, treat affected people as individuals or stakeholders, not as collective rights-holders who can refuse. An Indigenous-authored protocol, piloted on real AI deployment and data-centre decisions, would fill the empty indigenous × democracy cell.
openings.detail: The pieces exist on the map but nobody has packaged them as a process others can reuse. rising-voices' Chiapas programme (May 2026) concluded that speakers should decide whether and how AI enters their languages, and argued for pausing first. te-mana-raraunga-m-ori-data-sovereignty-network has the Principles of Māori Algorithmic Sovereignty and a record of legislative submissions. coding-rights' TRAMAS project maps conflicts over data centres in Latin American territories, where FPIC applies directly. old-ways-new advises Australian government. ada-lovelace-institute, which works on algorithmic impact assessment, could carry the result into standards. Success would be a protocol used in at least one real decision (a government automated decision-making system or a data-centre siting) and cited in AI impact-assessment guidance such as the EU AI Act's fundamental-rights impact assessments. Risks: FPIC is often hollowed out into mere consultation; its legal force varies by country; and it fits general-purpose frontier models poorly, so it should start with deployments and infrastructure tied to particular lands and communities. Its link to catastrophic risk runs through power and legitimacy (gradual disempowerment), not directly.
steps: Commission a short comparative study, written by Indigenous impact-assessment practitioners through GIDA or Te Mana Raraunga, of what transfers from Akwé: Kon and FPIC to AI systems and data infrastructure.
Pilot the draft protocol with Rising Voices' Chiapas network or a TRAMAS site facing a live data-centre or language-technology decision.
Take the tested protocol to the Ada Lovelace Institute and the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI for uptake in impact-assessment guidance.
openings.evidence: The indigenous × democracy cell is empty. rising-voices and coding-rights hold 2 of the map's 14 speed_of_wisdom badges. te-mana-raraunga-m-ori-data-sovereignty-network is coded 'policy'. The potential ring contains no FPIC or impact-assessment practitioner, and none was searched for.

openings.title: Community-governed red-teaming in African and Indigenous languages for safety institutes
openings.summary: Safeguards are weakest in low-resource languages. Masakhane, Te Hiku and Tattle hold the data, the communities and the skills to test them, but nothing on the map links them to the safety institutes' evaluation work, and no terms exist that keep red-team prompts under community control. A funded red-teaming and benchmark programme that respects data sovereignty would give this tradition its first solid foothold in assurance.
openings.detail: masakhane (over 1,000 participants, with a grant-making Hub funded by FCDO, IDRC and Gates) joined the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI in February 2026 and plans multilingual safety benchmarks. tattle-civic-tech (a bridge entry that draws on this tradition) already builds multilingual evaluations. te-hiku-media's Kaitiakitanga Licence is a template for keeping evaluation data out of training sets. Some multilingual testing already exists: Singapore's 2024-25 regional red-teaming challenge and the AI Safety Institute network's joint testing covered several Asian languages. I did not confirm in this pass which African or Indigenous languages they included. The opening is therefore the long tail of languages plus the governance terms, not multilingual testing as such. Success would be a benchmark in ten or more African and Indigenous languages, used in at least one safety-institute or lab pre-deployment evaluation, with contributors paid and the data licensed on community terms. Risks: communities doing unpaid safety work for labs; evaluation data leaking into training; capability gains for those languages that some communities may not want; and Te Hiku's technical output, which has slowed since 2023.
steps: Fund a safety red-teaming strand within the Masakhane African Languages Hub's next grant cycle, co-funded with IDRC AI4D and FCDO.
Draft a Kaitiakitanga-style licence for evaluation data with Te Hiku Media, so prompts and transcripts cannot be used for training.
Broker an agreement with UK AISI, or another institute in the network, to run the benchmark in pre-deployment testing, with CeRAI and Tattle as technical partners.
openings.evidence: The indigenous × assurance cell holds one entry (masakhane), the only assurance tag in the tradition. tattle-civic-tech is a bridge with indigenous as a secondary tradition. global-south-network-for-trustworthy-ai is a bridge. No safety funder appears among Masakhane's funders. angle_notes (b): nothing links planned multilingual benchmarks to the safety institutes' evaluation pipelines.

sector:democracy.overview: Democracy and collective intelligence brings two things to making AI go well. The first is the machinery of legitimacy for deciding together about AI: sortition, deliberative polling, consensus conferences and broad listening. The second is collective-epistemics tools: forecasting, argument mapping, fact-checking and provenance. The tradition has 68 home entries (12 core, plus Coefficient Giving counted as a generalist funder; 14 bridge, 37 adjacent, 5 potential), and 51 more organisations use it as a secondary tradition, most of them in law (Ada Lovelace, the Knight Institute, Weizenbaum) or elsewhere (MAI, Metagov, Toda). The main actors are CIP, the AI & Democracy Foundation, AOI and Odyssean at the core; Stanford DDL, DemocracyNext, CompDem/Polis and g0v/vTaiwan as bridges; a forecasting cluster (FRI, Metaculus, Sage, AI Impacts, Sentinel); and a dense band of adjacent civic-tech toolmakers (Harmonica, Dembrane, deliberAIde, Jigsaw, Make.org, DD2030/Team Mirai). Ten entries are on the aisafety.com map, the most of any Society & institutions tradition. Even so, only the forecasting half sits near the safety core; the deliberative half stays mostly adjacent.
sector:democracy.missing: The tradition's legitimacy methods have not reached the decisions the safety field cares about most. Only 6 of 69 entries use a catastrophic framing (5 of them forecasters), and only 2 deliberation organisations are core (Odyssean, whose assembly is still a proposal, and AIDF). No institution puts frontier-AI thresholds, pauses or AI moral status to representative publics, and nobody independently audits the AI mediators that now run public deliberations.

cell_notes.note: No ring cell for democracy has two or fewer entries (core 12, or 13 with Coefficient Giving; bridge 14; adjacent 37; potential 5), so these notes cover the thin cells inside each ring. Core leans heavily one way: 8 of 13 are forecasting/epistemics, 3 are CI tools (AOI, CIP, EIP) and only 2 are deliberation (odyssean-institute, ai-democracy-foundation). This looks like a real feature of the field, not a gap in the search. The collective and epistemics angles searched specifically for deliberation work framed as AI safety and found little: no dedicated funder for deliberative or pluralistic alignment, and OpenAI's Democratic Inputs was a one-off in 2023.

There are 14 entries, evenly split (5 tools, 4 deliberation, 5 epistemics), but fewer deliberation bridges are actually live. habermas-machine is dormant, with no commits since Jan 2025. global-coalition-for-inclusive-ai-governance is unverified, with no results since its Feb 2025 launch. The Allen Lab's GETTING-Plurality co-directorship ended in Jan 2026. That leaves roughly three active deliberation bridges: stanford-deliberative-democracy-lab, democracynext and vtaiwan-g0v. This is a real opening rather than a search artefact.

Adjacent is the densest ring: 37 entries, 14 of them CI-tool builders. The thin parts are geography and standpoint. Across all 69 entries there are none from Africa, Latin America or MENA, only 3 from Asia-Pacific (Taiwan, Japan, India), and 68 of 69 are tagged standpoint 'neither' (Tattle is the exception). Some of this is a search artefact, since searches were English-only. Some is probably real: the angle notes found the Global South present only through CIP's Global Dialogues, Aapti and Build Up. The tradition also has four empty problem cells (agency, ai_status, meaning, people). ai_status is the one worth acting on; see openings.

This is the thinnest cell: 5 entries (people-powered, democracy-x, society-library, centre-for-argument-technology-university-of-dun, internet-archive), none of them CI tools and only 2 in deliberation. It is mostly a search artefact. None of the field's main professional deliberation practitioners appear anywhere in the 717-line index: newDemocracy Foundation, MASS LBP, Involve, Sortition Foundation, Democratic Society, Kettering Foundation and Participedia. Nor does RadicalxChange, although the angle notes discuss it. Parliamentary technology-assessment offices were placed under arts. A targeted sweep would probably double this cell.

sector:democracy.key_insight: The safety field has taken up democracy's forecasting strand and left out its legitimacy strand. Seven of the ten democracy entries on the aisafety.com map are forecasting or collective-epistemics organisations (FRI, Metaculus, QURI, FLF, Sage, AI Impacts, Coefficient Giving), against only 1 of the 12 deliberation organisations (Odyssean), and 5 of the 6 entries that use a catastrophic framing are forecasters. The field has learned to ask crowds what will happen, but not to ask representative publics what should happen.

openings.title: Independent audit lab for AI facilitators and deliberation summarisers
openings.summary: AI now facilitates and summarises public deliberation, from Team Mirai's broad listening in Japan's parliament to EU-funded mass assemblies, but no one independently tests these mediators for steering, homogenisation, sycophancy toward majorities or capture by whoever writes the prompts. A small third-party lab that pairs safety-evals people with deliberation practitioners would fill this gap.
openings.detail: The map has 22 CI-tool entries, 14 of them adjacent builders shipping AI facilitators (harmonica, deliberaide, dembrane, deliberation-io, jigsaw, ai4deliberation, make-org, citizens-foundation, digital-democracy-2030-and-team-mirai). The best-known test, the Habermas Machine, did no fact-checking and raised homogenisation concerns. Academic groundwork exists: Stanford Digital Economy Lab's DeliberationBank and DeliberationJudge (Oct 2025) benchmarked 18 LLM summarisers and found that minority views are systematically under-represented. It is a static summarisation benchmark, though, not a standing auditor, and it does not test live multi-turn facilitation, persuasion or prompt capture. The failure modes are the same ones alignment worries about (sycophancy, manipulation, unfaithful reports), so AI in political roles makes a live testbed for oversight. Success would be a published audit protocol that governments and the UN Citizens' Track require when they procure tools, plus annual public audits of the main tools. The risks: vendors may refuse access, the market is small, and a clean audit could lend tools legitimacy too early.
steps: Fund a six-month threat-modelling project pairing DemocracyNext or Stanford DDL with an evals team (Sophron, CIP's Weval, or UK AISI's human-influence researchers).
Extend DeliberationBank (working with the deliberation-io team at Stanford and MIT) to multi-turn facilitation tests, with red-teams for steering, minority erasure and prompt capture.
Run the first audits, with consent, on open-source tools: Polis, Talk to the City/Kouchou AI, Harmonica and Dembrane.
Offer the protocol as a procurement condition to AI4Deliberation and the organisers of the UN Global Dialogue's Citizens' Track.
openings.evidence: There are 22 dem_tools entries, 14 of them adjacent builders. Only 15 of 69 entries address assurance, mostly fact-checking (full-fact, community-notes-and-the-ai-note-writer-pilot). habermas-machine is dormant, with its fact-checking gap still open. The collective angle's first 'missing bridge' is exactly this gap. A web check found only academic benchmarks (DeliberationBank, 2025), not a standing auditor.

openings.title: World Wide Views-style global deliberation on frontier-AI risk before May 2027
openings.summary: The UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance has a Citizens' Track that invites decentralised citizen assemblies to feed the second Dialogue (New York, 3-4 May 2027). Nothing ensures that frontier-AI thresholds or loss-of-control questions reach those agendas, or that the results can be compared across countries. Funding a synchronised deliberation in 30 or more countries on a single protocol, built on the Danish Board of Technology's World Wide Views method, would fill this.
openings.detail: The method already exists in this tradition. Democracy X (potential ring; formerly the Danish Board of Technology) ran World Wide Views on climate and biodiversity in dozens of countries at once. Missions Publiques, behind global-coalition-for-inclusive-ai-governance (unverified, no results since Feb 2025), ran the 'We, the Internet' global dialogue. Odyssean has an AI governance assembly proposal, and CIP's Global Dialogues are surveys, not deliberation. Connected by Data published design options for global citizen deliberation on AI in Sept 2024, and it and Ada pushed for the Citizens' Track. Success would be a comparable cross-national verdict on questions such as pause conditions, capability thresholds and who should decide, presented in May 2027. The risks: seven months is tight; cost is probably in the millions (I have not checked a budget); governments may ignore the results; and x-risk questions framed carelessly will look like advocacy, so briefing materials must be reviewed by both safety and ethics experts. I have not checked how the Citizens' Track is run beyond its published description.
steps: Contact the Citizens' Track organisers to learn the 2027 agenda, the submission format and whether frontier-risk questions are in scope.
Convene Democracy X, Missions Publiques, Odyssean, DemocracyNext and CIP to agree a common protocol and question set. int/a's Paris hub is close to Missions Publiques and Make.org and could host.
Fund national host partners, with deliberate inclusion of Africa and Latin America through People Powered's member network.
Commission balanced briefing materials, peer-reviewed from both the AI-safety and AI-ethics sides.
openings.evidence: Only 6 of 69 entries use a catastrophic framing. Core has just 2 deliberation entries (odyssean-institute, ai-democracy-foundation). global-coalition-for-inclusive-ai-governance is 'unverified', and democracy-x is 'potential' with light AI engagement. There are zero Africa or Latin America entries in the tradition. The collective angle's missing bridge 2 says frontier questions are rarely put to representative publics. A web check confirmed the Citizens' Track and the May 2027 date.

openings.title: Citizens' consensus conference on AI moral status and welfare
openings.summary: Policy on whether AI systems might matter morally is being shaped by labs and a few philosophers, while the public is only polled; I found no citizens' deliberation on AI moral status anywhere. A consensus conference, run by a practitioner that has just held one on animal welfare, would show what informed publics conclude and give welfare policy a basis in legitimacy.
openings.detail: The democracy x ai_status cell is empty for all 69 home entries. The nearest work comes from other traditions. Sentience Institute's AIMS survey has polled US attitudes in waves (2021, 2023, 2024), but that measures uninformed opinion. Eleos, NYU CMEP and the Digital Sentience Consortium do expert and funding work. CoSI, which has democracy as a secondary tradition, maps arguments about functionalism but does not deliberate. Democracy X ran a citizens' panel on pig welfare that produced eight recommendations in April 2026, so the method carries over directly to another contested question about non-human moral status. Success would be published recommendations from a randomly selected panel on concrete questions (welfare assessments, letting models end conversations, labelling companion AIs), heard from both functionalists and sceptics, with AIMS items used before and after to measure how deliberation shifts views. The risks: the topic is speculative and panels are sensitive to how experts frame it; the results could be used to inflate or dismiss claims; and mind attribution can harm users, so the panel should also hear from the minds-protection side (AI Psychological Research Coalition). The value to safety is uncertain, which is why confidence is only medium.
steps: Approach Democracy X and Eleos together to scope a Danish pilot.
Apply to the Digital Sentience Consortium / Longview Digital Minds RFP for funding.
Co-design measurement with Sentience Institute so that AIMS questions serve as the pre- and post-deliberation baseline.
If the pilot works, repeat it in one non-Western country to test cultural variation.
openings.evidence: democracy x ai_status is one of four empty problem cells for this tradition. ai_status has only 46 entries map-wide. democracy-x's recent work includes an April 2026 citizens' panel on pig welfare. A web search found deliberative polls on AI in the public sector, on high-risk AI and on creative industries, but none on AI consciousness or welfare.

openings.title: int/a sweep of missing deliberation practitioners, ending in shared standards
openings.summary: The tradition's potential ring holds only five entries. None of the field's main professional practitioners are on the map, and neither is any organisation from Africa, Latin America or the Middle East. int/a can close this gap within its own mapping project, then run one working session that ends with practitioners and AI tool builders co-signing minimum conditions for AI-assisted deliberation.
openings.detail: newDemocracy Foundation, MASS LBP, Involve, Sortition Foundation, Democratic Society, Kettering Foundation, Participedia and RadicalxChange are absent from the 717-line index. So are majority-world deliberative traditions with long track records: Brazilian participatory budgeting, Kerala's People's Plan, Kenya's constitutional duty of public participation, and Mongolia's deliberative-polling law. The angle notes say practitioners and the AI-safety deliberation-tool community 'work in parallel and rarely meet', and DemocracyNext objects to opinion-mapping tools such as Polis being called deliberation. That is exactly the disagreement a shared standard would settle. Success would be a verified democracy potential ring of 15-20 entries, profiled on the same schema, plus a short standard that openings 1 and 2 can use. The risks: a convening without a fixed output becomes talk; practitioners may see AI safety as a Silicon Valley concern; and English-only searching will repeat the blind spot unless the sweep runs in Portuguese, Spanish, Hindi and Japanese.
steps: Run a multilingual sweep, starting from Participedia's case database filtered for AI and from People Powered's member list.
Profile the finds on the existing schema and add them to the map.
Host a one-day workshop in Paris or London around a draft standard on minimum conditions for AI in deliberation, with Make.org, Café IA, Missions Publiques, DemocracyNext and tool builders.
Pass the agreed standard to the audit lab (opening 1) and the Citizens' Track organisers.
openings.evidence: Potential has 5 entries, with 0 CI tools and 2 deliberation. The region counts for the tradition are north_america 33, europe 17, uk_ireland 10, global 6, asia_pacific 3, and africa, latin_america and mena 0. Standpoint is majority_world for 1 of 69. Named practitioners are absent from index.txt (checked by search). The epistemics angle's gap 5 calls for linking deliberation practitioners with AI-safety tool builders.

sector:psych.overview: Psychology and cognitive science bring three things to AI going well. First, evidence on what AI does to human minds: clinical, developmental and relationship research. Second, methods for studying models as behavioural subjects: machine psychology, cognitive science and wisdom measurement. Third, care for the people doing AI-safety work. The map holds 65 organisations with psych as their home tradition (6 core, 15 bridge, 38 adjacent, 6 potential; 5 on the aisafety.com map) and 68 more that draw on it as a secondary tradition. The main actors form a clinical cluster (KCL Psychosis Studies, the Aarhus group, BIDMC Digital Psychiatry, Stanford Brainstorm, the Human Line Project, AIPRC), a youth cluster (Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute, everyone.AI, Fairplay, Young Futures), a few machine-psychology groups (Hagendorff's team at IRIS Stuttgart, Helmholtz HCA, Re-Align), Grossmann's Wisdom and Culture Lab, and UK AISI's Human Influence team. The tradition sits far from the core in its own right. Of the 65, 47 address protecting minds, 29 work by protecting their own constituency, and only 5 use a catastrophic framing. Psychology mostly reaches the core as a secondary ingredient of organisations homed elsewhere.
sector:psych.missing: No organisation on the map studies the psychology of the people and institutions steering AI: safety culture in labs, groupthink, escalation and how decision-makers perceive the race. Psych × security and psych × systemic are empty, and power has one entry (CHT). The taxonomy has no organisational or political psychology sub-tradition. Psychology on the map studies users, children and patients and looks after safety workers, but never examines the collective minds of the decision-makers. It also has no Majority-World organisation at all: 0 of 65.

cell_notes.note: No tradition × ring cell has two or fewer entries (6/15/38/6), so these notes cover the thin sub-tradition cells within each ring. Core has 6 entries but is hollow. Five are field-health services (rethink-wellbeing, upgradable, ai-safety-support, center-for-applied-rationality, fabric-european-summer-program-on-rationality) and the sixth is uk-ai-security-institute. Clinical, cognitive, developmental and relational psychology each have zero core entries. Among the five field-health entries, AISS has been dormant since July 2023, Upgradable has done little since February 2025, and CFAR has deliberately stepped back from AI framing. Part of this is a classification effect: 15 core organisations draw on psych as a secondary tradition (eleos-ai-research, cambridge-digital-minds, sophron-research, truthfulai, forecasting-research-institute, alignment-of-complex-systems-research-group) and are homed elsewhere. Still, no AI-safety organisation has been founded out of clinical or developmental psychology. This is a real opening.

15 entries, with three thin sub-cells. Relational has 1 (advancing-humans-with-ai-mit-media-lab), field health 1 (mental-health-navigator) and developmental 2 (common-sense-media, everyone-ai). The relational gap looks real. Attachment and intimacy science (kinsey-institute, mit-initiative-on-technology-and-self, association-for-the-advancement-of-affective-com) sits in adjacent or potential and describes companion harms without engaging alignment, even though UK AISI now uses the term 'socioaffective alignment'. The developmental figure is also real: only 2 of 18 developmental organisations reach bridge, and most youth work is literacy or protection.

38 entries, the bulk of the tradition, of which developmental alone accounts for 15. Field health is empty by definition: support for AI-safety workers is coded core or bridge, so this is not a gap. Relational has 2 (Turkle's initiative and Kinsey), which is probably partly a search artefact. Couples and attachment research centres and the research arms of dating platforms were not swept, yet they study human-AI romantic bonding with large samples.

6 entries, and every sub-tradition has two or fewer (clinical 1, cognitive 1, developmental 1, relational 1, social 2, field health 0). This is mostly a search artefact. The sweeps ran out of web searches, and whole professional fields leave no trace in the index: psychometrics, judgement and decision-making societies, organisational psychology (e.g. SIOP) and political psychology (e.g. ISPP). The blind-spot sweep also checked suicide-prevention and mental-health charities (Samaritans, Molly Rose Foundation, YoungMinds, IASP), found no AI work and did not list them, though they fit potential. The empty field-health cell is a real opening. Humanitarian staff-care practice and climate psychology (climate-psychology-alliance, homed under clinical) hold transferable know-how on distress under existential stakes, with no AI bridge.

sector:psych.key_insight: Psychology reaches the AI-safety core as an ingredient rather than a home. 15 core organisations draw on psych as a secondary tradition, against 6 core organisations whose home is psych, and 5 of those 6 are care services for the field's own workers: one has been closed since 2023 and one is largely inactive. Meanwhile the 14-organisation clinical cluster holds the best real-world evidence on a live model failure, sycophancy-driven delusion spirals: 185 analysed cases at KCL with the Human Line Project, and 38 harmful cases found in the records of 53,974 Aarhus psychiatric patients. None of the 14 is core or on the classic map, and all of them pass knowledge on only by protecting patients.

openings.title: Clinician reporting scheme that turns AI-linked psychiatric cases into model evals
openings.summary: Psychiatrists and therapists now see AI-associated delusions, mania and self-harm, but nothing lets them report cases in a standard way or routes those cases into model testing. A reporting scheme modelled on pharmacovigilance (the UK's Yellow Card, the FDA's adverse-event reporting system) would collect clinicians' reports, assess causality and turn de-identified conversation trajectories into multi-turn evals that AI Safety Institutes and labs run.
openings.detail: Pharmacovigilance is a mature discipline: clinicians report spontaneously, analysts look for signals across reports, and standard scales (such as WHO-UMC's) judge whether a drug caused a reaction. AI has no equivalent. The blind-spot sweep found no public-health body running sentinel surveillance of AI-associated presentations. Vanderbilt's 'algorithmovigilance' and Flinders' call for 'AI vigilance' are prototypes or proposals, and a quick search confirmed that governments do not require chatbot incidents to be reported. The evidence is piling up in separate places: Aarhus searched health records, KCL has 185 cases with the Human Line Project, AIPRC is collecting chat logs, and BIDMC built MindBench with NAMI. Meanwhile CHT wound down its psychosocial evaluation work on 1 October 2026, and labs take clinical input in-house (OpenAI's network of 170+ clinicians), which leaves no independent route. Success would be a standard report form used by clinicians in at least the UK, Denmark and the US, quarterly signal reports, and a consented, de-identified trajectory set that UK AISI's Human Influence team and Common Sense/Brainstorm turn into pre-deployment evals. The risks: transcript privacy and consent; self-selected reports, which show patterns but not prevalence; 'AI psychosis' is not a clinical diagnosis, so causal attribution is contested; and the scheme could duplicate ECRI's Problem Reporting Network or the news-based AI Incident Database, so it should feed into them, not compete.
steps: Convene Morrin and Pollak (KCL), Østergaard (Aarhus), Torous (BIDMC) and the Human Line Project to agree a minimum case-report form and a causality scale adapted from WHO-UMC. AIPRC's 18–20 October conference at UNC is a ready venue.

Pilot reporting through professional bodies that already engage with AI: BACP's roughly 75,000 members, the APsA Commission on AI's peer groups and the American Psychiatric Association's IT committee. Ask Mind's AI commission to recommend the scheme when it reports in 2027.
Fund replications of the Aarhus health-record screen in another Nordic register and one NHS trust, with better case definitions than keyword search.
Negotiate a data-sharing agreement with UK AISI and one lab so that consented, de-identified trajectories become held-out multi-turn sycophancy and delusion-amplification evals.
openings.evidence: Clinical sub-tradition: 14 organisations (4 bridge, 9 adjacent, 1 potential), 0 core, 0 on the classic map, all coded transfer = protecting. 29 of 65 psych organisations transfer by protecting. Aarhus found 38 harmful cases among 53,974 patients. KCL with the Human Line Project analysed 185 cases (September 2026). Blind spots: 'No public-health body runs syndromic or sentinel surveillance of AI-associated presentations.' CHT's psychosocial evaluations wound down on 1 October 2026.

openings.title: Clearance-aware therapy and duty-of-care standards for AI-safety staff
openings.summary: Psychological support built for AI-safety workers has shrunk while the field has grown, and nobody serves people whose stress is locked behind NDAs or infohazard rules. A small, clinically governed service would fill this gap: vetted therapists working under an agreed confidentiality framework, an AI-safety cohort in an existing peer programme, climate-café-style groups for AI distress, and exposure standards for red-teamers.
openings.detail: The core psych cell looks healthy at five field-health organisations, but it is fragile. AISS has been paused since July 2023 after founder burnout and slow funding decisions. Upgradable has done little since February 2025. CFAR has stepped back from AI framing and faces duty-of-care criticism. Mental Health Navigator runs on about £1,200 a year and does not vet its listings. Rethink Wellbeing is not AI-specific and is growing in low- and middle-income countries. Demand is clear: Bay Area therapists report that AI workers make up 40–80% of their caseloads, and a September 2026 LessWrong post names anticipatory grief and NDA-sealed stress as unmet needs. A quick search found no service for NDA-bound lab or AI Safety Institute staff. The knowledge exists elsewhere. Humanitarian staff-care practice (for example, the Antares Foundation's guidelines on stress in humanitarian workers) handles confidentiality, vicarious trauma and high stakes. Climate psychology (Climate Psychology Alliance cafés and facilitator training) handles group distress about an existential threat. Trust-and-safety work has protocols for exposure to harmful material, which evaluators handling CBRN or CSAM content lack. BACP published guidance on anxiety about AI's future in September 2026. Success would be a panel of vetted therapists, a recurring AI-safety cohort, groups in London, Berlin and Paris, and a duty-of-care standard that evals organisations adopt. The risks: labs may prefer in-house assistance programmes; the confidentiality framework is legally hard; reasonable concern should not be medicalised; and community-run programmes need clinical governance, as the CFAR and MAPLE controversies show.
steps: int/a convenes Rethink Wellbeing, Climate Psychology Alliance facilitators and BACP to design an AI-safety CBT Lab cohort and an 'AI café' format, and pilots both in London.

Commission an employment lawyer and a clinical supervisor to draft a confidentiality framework under which therapists can hear NDA-bound material, drawing on how security-cleared clinicians serve government staff.
Run a baseline field-wellbeing survey with clinically validated instruments, repeated yearly on the model of the Wellbeing Project's changemaker survey.
Seek two years of core funding (Coefficient Giving's Project Tailwind is the obvious first ask) so the service does not die of funding gaps, as AISS did.
openings.evidence: Core psych: 5 of 6 entries are field health, 0 field-health entries in potential. ai-safety-support is dormant, upgradable inactive since February 2025 and center-for-applied-rationality has changed course. mental-health-navigator runs on about £1,200 a year and does not vet listings. The angle notes record 40–80% AI-worker caseloads and that 'Garrison's CBR project is a ready-made... template that nobody has pointed at AI'. BACP published AI-anxiety guidance on 22 September 2026.

openings.title: Cross-cultural wisdom benchmark built from the Wise Judgment Consortium's data
openings.summary: Wisdom psychology has validated, cross-cultural measures of intellectual humility, perspective-taking and seeking compromise, and a 2026 paper by Grossmann and colleagues proposes AI wisdom benchmarks, but none has been built. Funding an open benchmark scored against human baselines from the 15-lab, five-continent consortium would give 'wise AI' a measurable target that is not tied to one culture.
openings.detail: Most values evaluations measure stated opinions or refusals. Wisdom science instead measures how people reason through hard, ambiguous problems, using coding schemes for recognising the limits of one's knowledge, considering change, weighing several perspectives and seeking resolution, with human norms from many countries. The Wisdom and Culture Lab (bridge) opened AI metacognition and expert-judgement programmes in September 2026. The Center for Practical Wisdom (potential, transfer none_yet) curates wisdom measures but has no AI work. The only operating flourishing benchmark, Gloo's, comes from a faith-tech company and uses Harvard's flourishing dimensions rather than wisdom-reasoning measures. Sophron Research builds third-party evaluations of reasoning quality and is a natural partner to host it. Success would be an open eval with held-out items and baselines from at least ten countries, used by UK AISI or a lab's model-spec team. The risks: models may learn to perform humility without the substance (Goodharting); measuring wisdom from the outside leaves out contemplative accounts of it; the cultural make-up of rater pools matters; and funding leans on Templeton sources.
steps: Fund a two-year postdoc joining Grossmann's lab with Sophron Research to turn wise-reasoning coding schemes into an automated, human-validated LLM eval.
Use consortium sites outside North America and Europe to collect human baselines and rater pools, so that the benchmark tests for Western-skewed defaults.
int/a convenes wisdom psychologists with contemplative researchers (Flourishing Intelligence Program, Jubilee Centre) to challenge the construct before release.
Release openly with a held-out test set and invite UK AISI to include it in its societal-resilience evaluations.
openings.evidence: Psych × values: only 6 of 65 organisations. wisdom-and-culture-lab is bridge, with new AI programmes posted 29 September 2026. center-for-practical-wisdom is potential with transfer none_yet. gloo-flourishing-ai-benchmark is homed in religion. A web check found that the July 2026 Waterloo paper 'suggest[s] benchmarks to measure AI wisdom' but none was released. 0 of 65 psych organisations have a Majority-World standpoint.

openings.title: Organisational and political psychology research on lab safety culture and race decisions
openings.summary: No organisation on the map applies organisational or political psychology to the labs and governments steering AI, although those fields have validated tools for measuring safety culture and long study of misperception and escalation in arms races. An independent research unit could survey safety culture across consenting labs and AI Safety Institutes with validated instruments benchmarked against nuclear and healthcare norms, and study how decision-makers perceive the race.
openings.detail: Lab safety culture is currently judged from outside: published frameworks, scorecards such as FLI's AI Safety Index and staff departures. A quick search found references to employee surveys inside some frameworks, but no independent use of validated organisational-psychology instruments. Other industries have such tools: nuclear operators' safety-culture assessments, AHRQ's hospital patient-safety-culture surveys and Edmondson's team psychological safety scales. Political psychology adds decades of work on groupthink, misperception and escalation that AI-race debates rarely draw on. The neighbouring traditions on the map stop short of this. The safety tradition (human-factors-and-ergonomics-society, resilience-engineering-association) studies operators and systems. SaferAI rates risk management. The AI Whistleblower Initiative supports individual employees. Intelligence Rising runs wargames whose behavioural data no psychologist analyses. Success would be a yearly anonymous culture survey with at least two labs and one AI Safety Institute taking part, and a published study of race perception among policy and lab staff. The main risks are access, since labs may decline; small samples that make anonymity hard; respondents gaming the survey; and overlap with existing ratings, so the work should feed SaferAI and similar raters rather than compete with them.
steps: Recruit one organisational psychologist with safety-culture experience from nuclear or healthcare and one political psychologist, and adapt a validated safety-culture instrument to AI development.
Pilot it with an AI Safety Institute first (UK AISI or Canada's), where public accountability makes access easier, then approach labs through their safety teams.
Partner with Intelligence Rising to add behavioural measures of escalation and trust to its wargames with policy audiences.
Share aggregate results with SaferAI and other raters so that inside measurements complement outside scores.
openings.evidence: Psych × security and psych × systemic are empty, and psych × power has 1 entry (center-for-humane-technology). No psych sub-tradition covers organisational or political psychology. Searching the index for 'safety culture', 'organisational psychology' and 'political psychology' returns no organisations. The angle notes call lab safety culture and system-safety methods 'almost absent from AI safety'.

sector:safety.overview: Safety and risk sciences bring the practical know-how that made aviation, nuclear power, medicine and finance safer: system-safety engineering and safety cases (centre-for-assuring-autonomy-university-of-york, mit-partnership-for-systems-approaches-to-safety, centre-for-software-reliability-city-st-george-s, safety-critical-systems-club, sae-g-34-eurocae-wg-114, ul-standards-engagement), measurement science (national-physical-laboratory, ptb-competence-centre-ai-and-metrology), incident learning (ai-incident-database, aiaaic, oecd-ai-incidents-and-hazards-monitor, ecri), risk management and insurance (saferai, centre-for-long-term-resilience, artificial-intelligence-underwriting-company, five actuarial bodies), and public health and biosecurity (johns-hopkins-center-for-health-security, securebio). The AI-safety field borrows more visibly from this tradition than from any other, yet most of it sits outside the field. Of 66 placed organisations, 9 are core, 27 bridge, 23 adjacent and 7 potential, and only 3 are on the aisafety.com map (CLTR, SaferAI, CARMA). Most of the bridges deal with narrow deployed autonomy such as cars, aircraft and clinical tools, not general-purpose systems, and 48 of 67 frame AI as a present harm. Biosecurity is the one strand that has fully crossed over: SecureBio runs pre-release evaluations of frontier models.
sector:safety.missing: The cultural and institutional half of safety science is missing. That means safety culture, just culture, high-reliability organising, confidential near-miss reporting, independent accident investigation and industry peer review on the INPO/WANO model. The tradition has no entries in the We quadrant, and only one of its entries (the CAIS course) aims at the people who build AI. Nobody yet applies these institutions to frontier developers.

cell_notes.note: The ring total (9) is above the threshold, but split by sub-tradition it is thin: safety_health has 0 core entries and safety_engineering has 3. The empty health cell is partly a matter of definitions. Biosecurity groups that do frontier work (securebio, johns-hopkins-center-for-health-security) count as bridge because they existed before their AI work. It is also a real opening: no organisation from public health or patient safety was founded to make AI go well. Nothing like an 'AI harms epidemiology' body exists, and the blind-spot sweep found no national public-health institute that treats AI as an exposure. The 3 engineering cores (gradient-institute, ai-security-initiative-center-for-long-term-cybe, the CAIS course) show that the system-safety community has produced almost no organisations native to AI safety. Its strongest voices, such as delft-algorithms-systems-safety-lab-tu-delft, stay bridge or critic. That is a real gap, not a search artefact.

The ring total is 7: 4 engineering, 1 risk (alliance-to-feed-the-earth-in-disasters) and 2 health (ihi-lucian-leape-institute, global-centre-for-preventive-health-and-nutritio). This is largely a search artefact. The safety-science sweep ran after the web-search budget was used up, and it names what it skipped: the safety-science groups at Lund, NTNU, Delft and Griffith, DNV, TÜV AI.Lab, and Japanese and Chinese assurance bodies. Nor were any of these profiled: nuclear operators' peer-review bodies (INPO, WANO), accident investigators (NTSB, AAIB, HSSIB), confidential reporting schemes (NASA ASRS, CHIRP), or process-safety bodies (CCPS, US CSB). Those hold exactly the institutional knowledge the tradition lacks on this map. Within the cell, though, the pattern is real: the leading safety-science bodies that were profiled (mit-partnership-for-systems-approaches-to-safety, resilience-engineering-association, safer-complex-systems) have no AI programme and are tagged as doors to open.

sector:safety.key_insight: Frontier AI safety has imported the safety tradition's artefacts (safety cases, risk thresholds, incident databases, the 'three lines' model) but not the institutions that make those artefacts work. Of 66 safety-tradition organisations, only 3 are on the aisafety.com map, none sits in the We quadrant, and none is a confidential reporting scheme, an accident-investigation body or a safety-culture peer reviewer for AI developers. Those three institutions did much of the work of making aviation, nuclear power and healthcare safe. Instead, the field's shared incident record rests on news reports and volunteers. The AI Incident Database put out a funding appeal in January 2026, AVID paused classification in March 2026, and AIAAIC has no paid staff. Meanwhile engineering-safety funders with deep pockets (Lloyd's Register Foundation's portfolio of about £300m, UL's $1.8bn commitment) fund almost no frontier work.

openings.title: Confidential near-miss reporting and accident investigation for frontier AI developers
openings.summary: Every AI incident record on the map is built from news reports or public submissions, so the near misses only lab and evaluation staff see are lost. Nothing like NASA's ASRS, the UK's CHIRP or ECRI's patient-safety reporting exists for AI. A neutral third party could run confidential, non-punitive reporting, and later independent investigation using the CAST method.
openings.detail: The four public incident systems (ai-incident-database with 1,700+ incidents, aiaaic with 2,000+, oecd-ai-incidents-and-hazards-monitor with about 18,000 detected automatically, and ai-vulnerability-database-ai-risk-and-vulnerabil) only see what reaches the press. CLTR's Loss of Control Observatory also draws on open sources. Mandatory regimes, such as California's critical-incident reporting for frontier developers and the EU AI Act's serious-incident duty, send reports to regulators. Aviation's experience is that blame-bearing channels suppress near-miss reports. the-ai-whistleblower-initiative supports people reporting wrongdoing, which is a different job from learning from honest errors. The idea of an ASRS for AI has been written up (Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, 2023), but my searches found nobody running one. ecri is the only working confidential reporting system on the whole map, with 8 million+ healthcare reports. Success would look like this: a trusted host that is neither lab nor regulator, non-retaliation terms signed by at least two developers, and a regular de-identified bulletin like ASRS's Callback. Later, an investigation function could grow, and so could an INPO-style peer-review role, which could become the operating-experience arm of the FINRA-style frontier standards body Demis Hassabis proposed in July 2026. The risks: low uptake without lab buy-in, legal discoverability of reports, hazardous details needing restricted tiers, and capture by the labs.
steps: Convene operators of ASRS, CHIRP and ECRI's Patient Safety Organization with AIWI and CLTR to draft a reporting protocol: de-identification, non-retaliation terms, and tiers for hazardous information.
Pilot with staff of AI-safety institutes, evaluation organisations and red-teaming contractors before approaching the labs, so a track record exists.
Train a small investigation team in CAST through MIT PSASS's free annual STAMP workshop.
Publish a quarterly de-identified bulletin of lessons, and use it to seek the labs' formal participation.
openings.evidence: There are 0 confidential reporting, accident-investigation or safety-culture peer-review bodies for AI among 715 mapped organisations. The four safety_risk incident databases are all built from media reports or submissions, and three are financially fragile: AIID's appeal in January 2026, AVID's pause in March 2026 and AIAAIC's volunteer model. ecri is the only confidential system on the map. The safety tradition has 0 entries in the We quadrant. The safety-science notes list this as gaps (a) and (b).

openings.title: Fellowship placing system-safety and human-factors engineers in AI-safety teams
openings.summary: The people who certify avionics software, write safety cases and study automation bias already belong to ready-made communities, but almost none of them work on general-purpose AI, and AI control and oversight research rarely cites them. A paid placement fellowship, co-funded by engineering-safety funders and AI-safety funders, would move them across, starting with the idea of minimising trust in the model and with the human-factors science of oversight.
openings.detail: Of the 33 safety-engineering organisations, only 3 are core. 18 are bridge, and those work almost entirely on cars, aircraft, robots and clinical tools. The safety-critical community's main conclusion is that ML components cannot be assured by classical means, so safety must come from defence in depth and highly assured guards around the model. Bloomfield and Rushby at centre-for-software-reliability-city-st-george-s make this case. It is close to AI-control research but rarely cited there, and witt-lab-university-of-oxford-moving-to-ucl shows why the question matters, since monitors can provably be evaded. Human-factors evidence on automation bias, skill decay and out-of-the-loop performance sits with human-factors-and-ergonomics-society and chartered-institute-of-ergonomics-human-factors, and is absent from the debate on scalable oversight. The money exists but is not connected: lloyd-s-register-foundation (a portfolio of about £300m, £10m to York CfAA) and UL Research Institutes fund engineering safety, while Coefficient Giving and SFF fund almost none of these bodies. Princint (formerly PIBBSS) shows that a fellowship can bring a discipline into AI safety. Success would mean 10 to 15 mid-career practitioners a year on six-month placements in AI-safety institutes, evaluation teams and control groups, producing joint work such as an STPA analysis of an agentic deployment. The risks: mismatched assumptions, since these methods assume bounded, specifiable systems; practitioners' day jobs; and the precedent of CASMI, a sponsor-funded hub that faded after 2024.
steps: Pitch a co-funded pilot to Lloyd's Register Foundation (its Foresight Review on the safe adoption of AI shows interest) and UL Research Institutes, alongside an AI-safety funder.
Recruit through the Safety-Critical Systems Club's 12 Nov 2026 seminar 'Safety Assurance for AI Systems', the MIT STAMP workshop and HFES's annual meeting.
Host the fellowship with Princint or York CfAA, with placements at UK AISI, NPL's Centre for AI Measurement and AI-control groups. int/a could hold the London cohort's meetings.
Set a first shared problem: a published STPA and safety-case review of one real agentic deployment.
openings.evidence: Of the 33 safety_engineering organisations, 3 are core and 18 bridge, mostly on narrow autonomy. 3 human-factors and resilience bodies are on the map (HFES, CIEHF, REA), and none is connected to oversight research. 7 entries are tagged as doors to open (partner). 11 safety organisations have a London presence, including SCSC, CSR, LRF and NPL. The notes list this as gaps (d), (e) and (h), and note that 'nobody owns STPA for AI agent ecosystems'.

openings.title: An epidemiology unit measuring AI harms at population level
openings.summary: Public health has the methods to tell whether chatbots and AI companions harm people at scale: surveillance, cohort studies, attributable-risk estimates and hazard classification. Yet no school of public health or national institute treats AI as an exposure. A dedicated unit would produce the population figures that company statistics and incident databases cannot give.
openings.detail: The safety_health sub-tradition has 10 entries and no core ones. Its AI-relevant work consists of single research lines inside other units. rand-health-care showed that published estimates of 'mental health use' of chatbots range from 0.01% to 72%, depending on definitions. flinders-health-and-medical-research-institute-f, a cancer-epidemiology lab, runs repeated audits of chatbot safeguards. department-of-affective-disorders-aarhus-univers uses health records. algorithmovigilance-programme-vanderbilt-univers monitors clinical models, and its founder left in September 2026. global-centre-for-preventive-health-and-nutritio has written one Lancet comment on chatbot advertising. The blind-spot sweep found no national public-health institute (RKI, RIVM, UKHSA, CDC and others) treating AI as a harm, no IARC-style hazard classification, and no WHO workstream on consumer chatbots. Papers now call AI a determinant of health, but nobody runs a programme on it. Success would mean a sentinel network of emergency and psychiatric services coding AI-associated presentations, an adolescent cohort study, and yearly attributable-risk estimates that regulators (us-fda-digital-health-advisory-committee) and labs can act on. The same surveillance machinery is early warning for slower, society-wide effects such as dependency. The risks: exposure is hard to define, data from companies is hard to get, and the work could feed a moral panic. It also overlaps with psychiatry groups such as stanford-brainstorm.
steps: Fund a three-year pilot unit at a school of public health that already has digital-epidemiology capacity.
Agree a standard definition of AI exposure with RAND Health and the Flinders group, so studies can be compared.
Set up a sentinel code for AI-associated presentations with a few emergency and psychiatric services, building on the Aarhus health-records method.
Negotiate privacy-preserving access to usage data with one chatbot provider.
openings.evidence: safety_health has 0 core entries and 10 in total. National public-health institutes were searched and none found working on this. The Flinders, RAND and Vanderbilt lines are each a strand of a non-AI unit. The safety-science notes list this as gaps (f) and (i). A quick check on 2026-10-04 found papers but no standing unit.

openings.title: Open catastrophe scenarios for correlated foundation-model failure, led by actuaries
openings.summary: Five actuarial bodies on the map run AI work, but all of it is about model governance and fairness. None applies the profession's methods for tail risk, accumulation and solvency to AI, even as insurers warn that reliance on three model providers makes agent liability behave like a catastrophe peril. An open set of disaster scenarios for foundation-model failure, built with the actuarial profession, would give AI safety a market-tested, priced view of correlated risk.
openings.detail: institute-and-faculty-of-actuaries, international-actuarial-association, society-of-actuaries-research-institute, casualty-actuarial-society and actuaries-institute are all adjacent and all frame AI as a present harm. The insurers price frequent, low-severity model error (armilla-ai, munich-re-aisure) or business-level risk (geneva-association). artificial-intelligence-underwriting-company is the exception: in September 2026 it proposed a mutual insurer for frontier labs. Outside the map, a quick search found the Lloyd's Market Association's first survey of AI loss scenarios (January 2026). It also found July 2026 notes from AIUC and the Cloud Security Alliance saying that over 80% of enterprise agent deployments run on three providers, which makes the risk an accumulation the market cannot yet price. So the commercial market has started. What is missing is a public scenario set backed by the profession, on the model of Lloyd's Realistic Disaster Scenarios, joined up with frontier-risk work: gradient-institute's 'monoculture collapse' failure mode, saferai's quantitative risk models, and bank-of-england and financial-stability-board's framing of frontier AI as a threat to financial stability. Success would mean an IFoA working party publishing open scenarios and accumulation measures that regulators use in stress tests and that labs' safety frameworks cite. The risks: insurers' commercial interests, scenarios that make extreme risk look insurable when the true tail cannot be priced, and a fast-moving commercial field.
steps: Propose an IFoA working party on catastrophic and accumulation risk from AI, building on the IFoA's September 2026 symposium and AI Manifesto.
Use int/a's London hub to convene IFoA, the Lloyd's Market Association, the Geneva Association, AIUC, Gradient Institute and Bank of England staff to agree three to five open scenarios.
Fund one actuarial researcher to cost the scenarios and publish the method and data.
Feed the results into SaferAI's risk models and CLTR's policy work, so frontier risk thresholds rest on a priced view of the tail.
openings.evidence: There are 5 actuarial bodies, all adjacent and all present-harms framed. The blind-spot sweep found 'no actuarial body working on catastrophic or long-horizon AI risk'. 4 insurers or insurance think tanks are on the map, only one of them frontier-explicit (AIUC). 5 of the 11 safety organisations in London are in finance, audit or actuarial work (IFoA, FCA AI Lab, IIA, ISACA, LRF).

sector:contemplative.overview: Contemplative and integral traditions bring first-person, practice-based knowledge of mind: what selfhood, attachment, attention and care are, and how they can be trained. They also bring a science of meditators, and the integral and metamodern milieu int/a itself comes from. The map holds 40 organisations with this home tradition (2 core, 11 bridge, 4 adjacent, 23 potential), plus 7 that draw on it secondarily, among them 84000, the Buddhism & AI Initiative and QRI. The part facing AI safety is about a dozen small, mostly new bodies: a science cluster turning Buddhist ideas into alignment targets (CSAS, FLIP, M3CS, Mathematical Metaphysics Institute, Groundless Alignment, Positive AI Labs) and a practice cluster forming AI builders (MAPLE, Wisdom + AI, Wisdom Beyond, Wisdom 2.0). It sits far from the core: none of the 40 is on the aisafety.com map, 33 frame the stakes as flourishing and only MAPLE as catastrophic, and half (20) belong to the integral and metamodern milieu, which gathers its own audience but has almost no AI-safety literacy.
sector:contemplative.missing: No contemplative claim about AI has yet been tested against the safety field's own evaluations. The seven groups that aim to change models rest on essays, prompting experiments and documents given to one lab, and the one group set up to build evaluations (positive-ai-labs) has published none. Behind this is money: the contemplative world's own funders make no AI grants, so its large institutions only convene, while its AI work depends on a few SFF and Templeton grants.

cell_notes.note: Two entries: positive-ai-labs (set up in 2025, nothing published yet) and groundless-alignment (SFF recommended $16k in 2026). This is mostly a real gap: very few organisations inside the AI-safety ecosystem are founded on contemplative practice. It is partly a tagging effect. The Buddhism & AI Initiative, the only classic-map entry with a contemplative strand, is homed in religion under rule B1. mathematical-metaphysics-institute is SFF-funded but tagged bridge. Researchers inside labs who draw on contemplative ideas don't count, because the unit is the organisation. A new core organisation is worth founding only if it does tested work (see the evaluation opening), not more convening.

Four entries (mind-life-institute, uva-contemplative-sciences-center, science-and-nonduality, world-institute-for-science-religion-and-culture), against 23 potential. That is a hollow middle: organisations either take up an explicit alignment frame (11 bridge) or keep AI to one-off events. Part of this is a search artefact. Large contemplative-science centres such as UW-Madison's Center for Healthy Minds don't appear in the discovery notes. Asian Buddhist, Indian and Christian contemplative networks were covered thinly (the blind-spot notes list Thailand, India, and CAC and Contemplative Outreach behind Cloudflare as thin or unverified). Part is real: the angle notes found no AI programming at about 25 retreat and contemplative centres (Omega, Spirit Rock, Upaya, Naropa, Kripalu and others), and only one AI item each at Plum Village and Oxford Mindfulness.

sector:contemplative.key_insight: 23 of the tradition's 40 organisations (58%) are only potential partners, the highest share of any of the 14 traditions (life sciences come next at 37%). The funders who could change that make no AI grants: Fetzer, Kalliopeia, 1440, Hemera, Templeton Religion Trust, and Mind & Life's own grant line. The well-funded institutions (Garrison about $4.8M in revenue, Presencing about $4.5M, Mind & Life about $3.5M, SAND about $2.7M) convene. The tradition's actual AI-safety work is carried by about a dozen tiny groups, and only four of the 40 profiles name SFF, LTFF or a Templeton body as a funder.

openings.title: Test contemplative 'no-self' training against self-preservation and sycophancy evaluations
openings.summary: Contemplative groups claim that training AI in non-attachment to self, paired with care, would remove the self-preservation drive behind shutdown resistance and deception, but nobody has tested this beyond prompting. A pre-registered fine-tuning study against the safety field's own shutdown, agentic-misalignment and sycophancy tests would show whether the idea has substance.
openings.detail: CSAS proposes the bodhisattva as an alignment target and no-self as a remedy for self-preservation incentives, and with 84000 it has passed documents to Anthropic for training. The 'Contemplative AI' paper from FLIP and M3CS researchers reports gains on AILuminate and a Prisoner's Dilemma, but only from prompting. Mainstream safety now measures self-preservation concretely: Palisade's 2025 shutdown-resistance study, Anthropic's agentic-misalignment tests across 16 models, and a 2026 arXiv paper quantifying self-preservation bias. A June 2026 NYU paper ('Existential Indifference') argues for building systems with no self-preservation, but grounds this in the phenomenology of suicidal states, not in traditions that have long trained non-attachment alongside care. Success would be a public, replicable result, positive or negative, on open-weight models, with corpora and code released so that an evaluator such as UK AISI could rerun it. Risks: models may learn the vocabulary of no-self without changing behaviour. Less self-concern might also mean less resistance to misuse or to tampering with the model's values, so that must be measured too. And a thin 'Buddhism as data' approach would misrepresent the tradition, so scholars must co-design the corpus.
steps: Convene researchers from CSAS, FLIP and M3CS with one evaluation team to fix a pre-registered protocol: an open-weight model fine-tuned on a contemplative corpus, compared with matched controls (generic ethics text, an 'existential indifference' corpus, and no fine-tuning).

Run Palisade-style shutdown tasks, agentic-misalignment scenarios, standard sycophancy evaluations and a multi-agent social-dilemma suite, with probes that tell real behavioural change from mere use of contemplative vocabulary.

Publish everything, null results included, with corpora and code. Offer the protocol to UK AISI's Alignment Project and to Positive AI Labs, which promised wisdom-sourced datasets but has released none.
Fund it as a 12-month project for two or three people. SFF already funds two contemplative-alignment groups, so it is the natural first funder.
openings.evidence: Only 1 of the 40 contemplative organisations has an evaluation role (positive-ai-labs), and it has published no datasets. The 7 entries tagged 'into the model' rest on essays, prompting-only experiments and documents shared with one lab: center-for-the-study-of-apparent-selves, flourishing-intelligence-program-centre-for-euda, monash-centre-for-consciousness-and-contemplativ, mathematical-metaphysics-institute, groundless-alignment, institute-for-developmental-philosophy and positive-ai-labs. Contemplative x assurance has a single entry; contemplative x multi_agent and contemplative x security are empty. Compassion-focused evaluation exists elsewhere (compassion-aligned-machine-learning, gloo-flourishing-ai-benchmark), but none of it targets self-preservation.

openings.title: A contemplative-science grant call on AI safety problems, co-reviewed by safety researchers
openings.summary: The contemplative world's grant-makers have money and review machinery but fund nothing on AI, while contemplative alignment work depends on a handful of SFF and Templeton grants. A pooled call, led by Mind & Life with other contemplative funders, that poses specific AI-safety problems in contemplative-science terms would move that money.
openings.detail: Mind & Life named AI and technology a priority in its 2025 strategy and held Dialogue XXXIX on AI in October 2025. But it has no AI grant line, none of its recent small grants is on technology, and its 2026 Summer Research Institute was on depolarisation. Discovery found no AI grantmaking at Fetzer, Kalliopeia, 1440, Hemera (which spends out in 2028) or Templeton Religion Trust. The crossover funding that does exist comes from SFF (mathematical-metaphysics-institute, $126k in 2026; groundless-alignment, $16k) and from Templeton bodies: TWCF funded CSAS, and JTF runs a Future of Intelligence venture. There are concrete problems to pose: contemplative evaluations of model behaviour, users' dependence on AI, the formation of AI researchers, and first-person methods for questions about AI interiority. Success would be a first round of small grants whose outputs AI-safety researchers actually cite. Risks: these funders and their grantees mostly reject control-and-catastrophe framings (Garrison's AI conference set out to go 'beyond' them), and without safety co-reviewers the grants could buy more dialogue rather than tested work.
steps: int/a writes a short brief that restates five or six AI-safety problems in contemplative-science language, naming for each the teams on this map who could take it up.
Take the brief to Mind & Life's programme staff (its grant system had funded more than 270 projects by 2020) and propose a pilot round of small grants with an AI-safety co-reviewer on each panel.
Ask Fetzer, 1440 or Templeton Religion Trust to pool funds, and SFF or JTF's Future of Intelligence venture to match, so the call is not one funder's experiment.
Commission a one-year review of what the grants produced, published for both communities.
openings.evidence: The discovery notes found no AI grantmaking at Fetzer, Kalliopeia, 1440, Hemera or Templeton Religion Trust. mind-life-institute has a stated AI priority but no grant line. Only four of the 40 profiles name SFF, LTFF or a Templeton body as a funder (mathematical-metaphysics-institute, groundless-alignment, center-for-the-study-of-apparent-selves, perspectiva). 23 of the 40 entries are potential, and 19 transfer only by convening their own community.

openings.title: Contemplative resilience training for AI policy staff, with a safeguarding standard
openings.summary: The contemplative programmes aimed at AI people are small, expensive, closed or under public allegations, while programmes with a track record in parliaments and Congress do no AI work. Adapting those programmes for staff of AI safety institutes and AI policy teams, and giving the field a safeguarding standard for the contemplative programmes it refers people to, would fill both gaps.
openings.detail: The Mindfulness Initiative has trained roughly 300 politicians and published a 2026 guide to mindfulness in political institutions. Garrison's Contemplative-Based Resilience course has reached US Congressional staff through the House Center for Well-Being since 2022. The Wellbeing Project runs an 11,000-respondent wellbeing survey and a track in which 45 foundations are changing their practice. None of the three has any AI work. On the AI side, MAPLE's fellowship costs $3,000 a month and faces allegations (2021, and July 2026) of high-control dynamics, which MAPLE disputes. Wisdom + AI retreats start at £1,680 in a closed network, Wisdom Beyond is moving to invite-only, and Wisdom 2.0 is a private events business. The psychology-based field-health services (rethink-wellbeing, upgradable, ai-safety-support, mental-health-navigator) are built for the AI-safety community, and none is tagged contemplative. Success would be a measured pilot inside one AI safety institute and a short safeguarding standard that referrers actually use. Risks: effect sizes in mindfulness research are modest; there is the 'McMindfulness' worry that training helps people tolerate pressures that ought to change; and civil servants may not take it up.
steps: Pilot a short CBR or Mindfulness Initiative course with staff of one AI safety institute, measured with the Wellbeing Project's survey instrument. UK AISI, the Mindfulness Initiative and int/a's hub are all in London.

int/a drafts a safeguarding checklist for contemplative programmes that serve AI people, with clinicians from the psychology field-health groups: governance independent of the teacher, complaint routes, no discouraging of outside therapy, and norms on sleep and fees. Offer it to the organisations that refer people.
Run a first field-wide wellbeing survey of AI-safety and AI-policy workers with the Wellbeing Project, to replace unverified burnout figures such as the 59% quoted at discovery.
openings.evidence: 12 of the 40 contemplative entries address the people doing the work. The five working directly with AI builders are wisdom-ai, wisdom-beyond, monastic-academy-for-the-preservation-of-life-on, wisdom-2-0 and connecting-intelligence, the last with no outputs. the-mindfulness-initiative, the-wellbeing-project and inner-development-goals are potential with transfer none_yet, and garrison-institute is potential.

openings.title: A contemplative-science trial against AI companion dependency and AI anxiety
openings.summary: Evidence of dependence on AI companions is accumulating, and contemplative science has trialled interventions for compulsive use and anxiety, but nobody on the map has tested them on AI use. A pre-registered trial at a contemplative-science centre, plus design guidance for companion products, would make the link.
openings.detail: UVA's Contemplative Sciences Center has launched an AI + Human Flourishing Initiative, opening with a symposium on AI anxiety on 18-19 November 2026, but it has no research outputs yet and no AI-safety specialists. SIYLI runs a single 'Addressing AI Anxiety' workshop. Friends of Attention has practical exercises for defending attention but no AI work. Arising has named the pattern ('machinal bypass') in an essay. The problem is documented: Drexel research on teens' dependence on Character.AI, and an MIT Media Lab and OpenAI study linking prolonged daily voice use with worse wellbeing. Tested starting points exist in mindfulness-based relapse prevention and mindfulness programmes for problematic smartphone use. One quick search found studies of mindfulness delivered by ChatGPT, but no trial of contemplative training to reduce dependence on AI. Success would be a published trial plus a short set of design patterns (pauses, friction, reflective prompts) that companion developers and evaluators such as Common Sense Media could adopt. Risks: psychology (38 adjacent entries) may get there first, leaving the contemplative angle little to add; effects may be small; and teaching users to cope must not stand in for holding developers to account.
steps: Approach UVA's CIRCL lab and CCARE to co-design a trial of a four-to-eight-week contemplative protocol for young adults who report heavy companion-chatbot use, with Stanford Brainstorm or the AI Psychological Research Coalition supplying measures of dependence.
Pre-register the outcomes: hours of use, a validated dependence scale, loneliness and anxiety, all measured again at follow-up.
