Turn the results, together with Friends of Attention's exercises, into design guidance for companion apps, and offer it to Common Sense Media for its AI risk assessments.
openings.evidence: 11 contemplative entries address protecting minds, but only uva-contemplative-sciences-center (new, no outputs) and search-inside-yourself-leadership-institute (one workshop) touch AI use directly. friends-of-attention has transfer none_yet. The evaluators of AI harms to minds sit in psychology (common-sense-media, stanford-brainstorm, ai-psychological-research-coalition).

sector:formal.overview: The formal tradition brings mathematics, theoretical physics, theoretical computer science, logic, statistics, and decision and game theory to AI safety. It uses them to define, explain and verify what AI systems are and do. The main actors are a dense cluster around Principles of Intelligence and Iliad (aixi-labs, stormglass-ai-safety-institute, alignment-journal, affine-network, dovetail); well-funded theory labs (resolution, mathematical-ai-safety-institute, simplex, computational-rational-agents-laboratory); ARIA's category-theory programme (aria, topos-institute, glaive); cooperative game theory (foundations-of-cooperative-ai-lab, modeling-cooperation, the Teesside group, the PIK group at Potsdam); and an outer ring of statistics, metrology and decision-science societies. It sits closer to the AI-safety core than any other tradition: half of its 30 organisations are core and a third are on aisafety.com's map, against 14% and 9% across the whole map.
sector:formal.missing: The missing formal disciplines are the ones aimed at how people decide rather than at the model itself: social choice, decision analysis under deep uncertainty, and measurement science. They sit in the potential ring or are absent from the map. No formal-rooted organisation works on democratic voice, meaning, or the moral status of AI.

cell_notes.note: Only one entry (munich-center-for-mathematical-philosophy-lmu). This is mostly an artefact of the taxonomy and the search, with a smaller real gap behind it. The taxonomy files formal work on AI's social effects under other traditions: fairness and accountability under law, markets and power under economics, and the metrology institutes (national-physical-laboratory, ptb-competence-centre-ai-and-metrology, lne-laboratoire-national-de-m-trologie-et-d-essa) under safety. The statistics sweep ran with no web searches, and whole communities are absent from index.txt: the theoretical computer science of responsible computing (the FORC symposium, the Simons Institute, differential-privacy groups) and the Leiden Declaration on AI and Mathematics, which blind_spots.md found but which was never added. The real gap is narrower. Few formal-discipline bodies use their own tools to study what AI does to their field or to society. The mathematics community's response to automated proof is the strongest candidate to fill this cell.

Seven entries, so not thin by count, but narrow. Six are statistics, decision-science or metrology societies (american-statistical-association, informs-decision-analysis-society, society-for-decision-making-under-deep-uncertain, european-network-for-business-and-industrial-sta, euramet-european-metrology-network-for-mathemati, international-society-for-bayesian-analysis). The seventh is simons-collaboration-on-the-physics-of-learning. No mathematics, logic or theoretical-CS learned society appears (IMU, LMS, AMS, SIAM and SIGACT all return nothing). SIAM, IMS and INFORMS's main sites could not be read behind bot walls, so this is partly a search limit. The Simons collaboration ($2M a year, no safety framing) is the obvious way to deepen the formal core, but that core is already the best-funded part of the map. It is therefore a weaker bet for widening the field than the statistics and decision-science entries.

Seven entries, but three of them (topos-institute, glaive, basis-research-institute) owe their AI-safety work mainly to ARIA's Safeguarded AI programme. glaive has already moved to AI-for-mathematics tooling since its ARIA award closed. The bridge is real but fragile: it depends on one public funder, whose priorities narrowed to cybersecurity in 2025-26.

Not thin (15 entries), but undercounted. cooperative-ai-foundation, which the taxonomy itself gives as an example for this tradition, is in roster_final.json but missing from index.txt, so formal x multi_agent (7) understates cooperative-AI work. MIRI, CLR, Atlas Computing and the Beneficial AI Foundation are on aisafety.com's map but not on this one.

sector:formal.key_insight: The AI-safety field already owns the formal tradition, and the money follows. Of its 30 organisations, 15 are core (50%, against 14% map-wide), 10 are on aisafety.com's map (33%, against 9%) and only one is adjacent (3%, against 45%). In 2026, Coefficient Giving alone committed about $170M to two formal-core labs (Resolution $160M, MAISI $10M), close to the whole $200M Project Tailwind call. Twenty-one of the 30 apply their knowledge to the model itself, and 20 work on understanding AI and agency. The formal disciplines aimed at human decisions (statistics, metrology, decision analysis, social choice) sit in the potential ring. That is where new funding would actually widen the field.

openings.title: A social choice programme for aggregating public input into AI specifications
openings.summary: No formal-rooted organisation on the map works on democratic voice: formal x democracy is empty, and only two formal entries address what AI should value. A standing programme would put social choice theorists to work on how labs and deliberation projects turn conflicting public input into model specifications and constitutions.
openings.detail: Social choice theory has decades of results on aggregating conflicting preferences, from impossibility theorems to proportional rules. The relevant people are on the map but not connected: Christian List at munich-center-for-mathematical-philosophy-lmu, Jobst Heitzig's social-choice and agency-preserving work at potsdam-institute-for-climate-impact-research, Conitzer's foundations-of-cooperative-ai-lab, and Topos's co-specification tools (topos-institute). The deliberation organisations that already feed models (collective-intelligence-project, computational-democracy-project, meaning-alignment-institute) are rooted in democracy or philosophy, not formal theory. Academic interest exists: the ICML 2026 Pluralistic Alignment workshop, a June 2026 survey on alignment from social choice perspectives, and the PlurVA-LLM workshop in November 2026. But nothing sustains it between conferences, and ARIA's pages no longer mention the deliberative-specification strand of Safeguarded AI (inferred, not confirmed). Success would be a group of three to five researchers paired with one deliberation organisation, publishing aggregation rules with stated guarantees (what minorities are assured of, where strategic manipulation is possible) that a lab or an AI safety institute adopts. Risks: lab-internal 'collective alignment' teams may already crowd the space, the theory may produce impossibility results that practitioners ignore, and some of this work may already be filed under the democracy tradition.
steps: int/a convenes a two-day working session pairing List (MCMP), Heitzig (PIK) and Conitzer's group with CIP, CompDem and MAI, all working on one concrete question: how a specific published public-input process should aggregate its results.
A funder offers a two-year pilot (two postdocs) at MCMP or PIK, on condition that a deliberation partner co-designs the problem.
Ask ARIA whether Safeguarded AI's sociotechnical specification strand has been dropped; if it has, offer topos-institute a bridge grant to adapt CatColab for stakeholders to specify jointly.
List the authors of the 2026 social-choice-and-alignment papers and check which of them have institutional backing beyond a single paper.
openings.evidence: formal x democracy is an empty cell. formal x values has only two entries (computational-rational-agents-laboratory, potsdam-institute-for-climate-impact-research). topos-institute is the only formal-home organisation with democracy as a secondary tradition, and it is tagged assurance and epistemics. The discovery notes say ARIA's current page no longer mentions deliberative specification work.

openings.title: Deep-uncertainty decision methods to stress-test frontier safety frameworks' if-then thresholds
openings.summary: Frontier safety frameworks rest on if-then commitments, which work like the signposts and triggers of adaptive planning, yet the decision scientists who built that method for flood defence and climate policy have no AI programme. A pilot would apply robust decision making, adaptive pathways and structured expert elicitation to one published framework.
openings.detail: The DMDU Society (society-for-decision-making-under-deep-uncertain) and the INFORMS Decision Analysis Society (informs-decision-analysis-society) hold the toolkit: dynamic adaptive policy pathways, robust decision making, value-of-information analysis and multi-attribute trade-offs. Both are in the potential ring and mention AI only in meeting themes. The discovery sweep found no structured-expert-judgement group (Cooke's Classical Model, IDEA, SHELF) working on AI. A few 2026 arXiv papers have started applying deep-uncertainty language to frontier AI policy, but no organisation owns the work. On the AI side, saferai already rates frontier frameworks, center-for-ai-risk-management-alignment works on risk management, and society-for-risk-analysis is a bridge. Success would be a published stress-test of one developer's thresholds across many plausible futures, showing which triggers fail and which signposts are missing, taken up in SaferAI's ratings or by an AI safety institute. Risks: developers may not disclose enough to make the analysis concrete; practitioners from climate and water may lack AI fluency and produce generic results; and a field that relies on forecasting may treat the work as redundant with probabilistic forecasts.
steps: Fund a six-month pilot pairing two DMDU practitioners (from the TU Delft or RAND lineage) with SaferAI to stress-test one published frontier safety framework.
Propose an AI track for the DMDU Society's 2027 annual meeting and a special issue of the journal Decision Analysis.
Run one structured expert elicitation on a dangerous-capability threshold using Cooke's Classical Model with calibration questions, and compare the results with forecasting-platform estimates.
openings.evidence: Both decision-science entries are in the potential ring with 'convening' transfer and no AI programme. blind_spots.md rates decision-analysis communities as thin and lists expert-elicitation communities as searched with none found. formal x epistemics has only four entries.

openings.title: Statisticians and metrologists set uncertainty reporting for dangerous-capability evaluations
openings.summary: Statistics and measurement-science bodies now run AI programmes, but all of them frame AI as sector regulation or present harms. Meanwhile, verdicts on whether a frontier model crosses a dangerous-capability threshold often rest on a few runs with no stated uncertainty. A secondment programme and a reporting protocol in the style of the GUM (the metrology Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement) would bring their methods to the evaluations that trigger safety commitments.
openings.detail: The royal-statistical-society's AI Task Force has an evaluation subgroup and argues that regulating AI is largely a statistical evaluation problem. european-network-for-business-and-industrial-sta has a Reliability and Safety group and a 2027 meeting on design of experiments for AI validation. euramet-european-metrology-network-for-mathemati links 14 national metrology institutes. national-physical-laboratory opens its Centre for AI Measurement in November 2026, and ptb-competence-centre-ai-and-metrology already issues test-dataset specifications. NIST published a report on statistical models for AI evaluation (AI 800-3) in February 2026. None of these bodies works with uk-ai-security-institute or independent evaluators on the evaluations that decide whether a frontier model crosses a dangerous-capability threshold. Success would be a short, citable protocol for reporting uncertainty and traceability in such results, adopted by at least one AI safety institute and one developer. Risks: NIST and NPL may do this themselves, making an outside effort redundant; and the harder problem may be construct validity (does the test measure the risk?) rather than sampling error, which statistics alone does not fix.
steps: Fund three or four six-month secondments of industrial statisticians or metrologists, recruited through the RSS AI Task Force and ENBIS's Reliability and Safety group, into UK AISI or an independent evaluator.

Ask NPL's Centre for AI Measurement and PTB AI-Met whether frontier dangerous-capability evaluations are in their scope; if not, convene them with UK AISI to draft a GUM-style supplement for capability thresholds.
Re-analyse a handful of published dangerous-capability results with mixed-effects models to show how often a threshold verdict falls inside the error bars; this makes the case concretely.
openings.evidence: Statistics and metrology bodies make up four of formal's seven potential entries (american-statistical-association, european-network-for-business-and-industrial-sta, euramet-european-metrology-network-for-mathemati, international-society-for-bayesian-analysis), with royal-statistical-society in the bridge ring. All five are framed as present harms. blind_spots.md calls metrology for AI evaluation 'a clear blind spot'. The statistics sweep ran without web search, so recall is weak.

openings.title: Convene mathematicians on what automated proof means for human understanding
openings.summary: The formal tradition has no entry on meaning, dignity or formation, yet mathematicians are living through the automation of proof now and have begun to respond as a community. int/a could convene them on what is lost and what is kept when machines verify results no human understands, an early, observable case of gradual epistemic disempowerment.
openings.detail: The Leiden Declaration on AI and Mathematics (June 2026, endorsed by the International Mathematical Union) addresses epistemic reliability, dependence on proprietary tools and autonomy. The discovery sweep found it, but it is not on the map. Funding is pulling formal researchers towards AI-for-mathematics: glaive moved from ARIA safety verification to theorem-proving tactics, and fields-institute-centre-for-mathematical-ai runs AI-for-maths alongside its safety strand. The Simons Institute's September 2026 working-group report on AI and theoretical computer science shows a neighbouring community facing the same shift. The safety field treats all this as a capability story. It is also the clearest live case of people relying on knowledge whose understanding they have lost, which the gradual-disempowerment work of alignment-of-complex-systems-research-group and the formal-contemplative work of mathematical-metaphysics-institute both touch. Success would be a recurring dialogue whose essays or report are cited in gradual-disempowerment and scalable-oversight discussions, and a few mathematicians taking up oversight of superhuman reasoning as a research question. Risks: confidence is low that this changes safety practice; mathematicians may treat it purely as a professional or sociological matter; and philosophy of mathematics may already cover the ground.
steps: Approach the Leiden Declaration's organisers and the Fields Centre for Mathematical AI to co-host a small dialogue in 2027 with ACS's gradual-disempowerment researchers.
Commission three essays from working mathematicians on checking an AI proof they do not understand, and what oversight of superhuman reasoning would require.
Add the Leiden Declaration and similar professional responses to the map, so that the formal x meaning cell is not empty by omission.
openings.evidence: formal x meaning is an empty cell, and the adjacent ring has a single formal entry. The Leiden Declaration is recorded as found in blind_spots.md but is absent from index.txt. glaive's profile documents the drift from safety verification to AI-for-mathematics tooling.

sector:law.overview: Law brings the tools societies already use to hold powerful actors to account: liability and litigation, human-rights law and due diligence, children's-rights design codes, treaties and whistleblower protection. Through STS and sociology it also brings field methods for studying how technologies are built and used. It is the largest tradition on the map (91 placed organisations, or 93 profiles counting the generalist funders CIFAR and Humanity AI). Its main actors include the Tech Justice Law Project, Hadfield's Normativity Lab, OHCHR B-Tech, the Council of Europe, CAIDP, 5Rights, Data & Society, the Ada Lovelace Institute, the Oxford Internet Institute and Schwartz Reisman, with Humanity AI, the European AI & Society Fund and IDRC's AI4D as funders. It sits far from the safety core: 62 adjacent, 19 bridge, 8 potential and only 2 core (AIWI and ILINA), with 3 on the aisafety.com map (AIWI, ILINA, PAI). Justice is the primary problem for 43 of 93, but bridges are forming through Global South safety work (GCG, Digital Futures Lab, the Global South Network) and through the UN rights chief's September 2026 letter warning frontier AI companies of existential risks.
sector:law.missing: No legal organisation yet carries the rights-law tools (due diligence, litigation and remedies, treaty monitoring, statutory regulators) into frontier-safety practice. Nothing links the x-risk legal groups on the classic map (LawAI, CLAIR, LASST, Legal Safety Lab) with the 62 adjacent rights organisations. The gap is widest in Latin America: all 10 Latin American organisations on the whole map are adjacent, 8 of them rooted in law, and the regional safety groups that grew out of EA (LANAIS, BAISH, the LATAM fellowship) do not appear to work with them.

cell_notes.note: Two placed entries: the-ai-whistleblower-initiative and ilina-program. CIFAR's CAISI programme is also core but counted as a generalist funder. Part of this is a scope choice. The aisafety.com map's own legal organisations (LawAI, CLAIR, LASST, Legal Safety Lab) come from inside the x-risk world and apply US frontier-regulation and liability law rather than an outside tradition, so they are not counted here. Legal Safety Lab was added in one sweep with its status unclear, and it is missing from the index. The opening is still real in a narrower sense. No core organisation carries human-rights law, children's-rights law, Global South legal experience or STS into safety work. Only 2 of the 93 law profiles (ILINA, AI Rights Institute) are framed around catastrophic risk, and only AIWI reaches the people inside labs.

Eight entries, so not strictly under the threshold, but thin for the map's largest tradition: 9% of law entries are potential, against 16% map-wide. Five are STS learned societies or history projects (EASST, 4S, CASTAC, Cambridge Histories of AI, Deutsches Museum); the others are Library Futures, the Center for Genetics and Society and the Future Generations Commissioner for Wales. This is probably a search artefact. Nobody swept law-reform commissions (the Law Commission of England and Wales, for example, published an AI discussion paper in 2025), ombudsmen, national human rights institutions other than DIHR, judicial-training bodies, access-to-justice groups, arbitration bodies, or future-generations offices outside Wales. These hold transferable methods such as liability reform, complaint handling and judicial fact-finding, and deserve one targeted sweep.

sector:law.key_insight: Law is the map's largest tradition (91 of 707 placed organisations), yet its weight sits almost wholly outside the safety frame. It has only 2 core entries, and 2 of its 93 profiles are framed around catastrophic risk against 52 framed around present harms. 56 of 93 transfer their work into institutions, 4 into the model, and just 1 (AIWI) into the people building AI. The legal tools are already built, but they point at present harms. The law entries on the classic map all come from inside x-risk, so two legal communities work side by side without meeting. The first clear crossing came from the adjacent side: in September 2026 the UN High Commissioner asked frontier AI companies for human-rights due diligence that includes safety standards and incident reporting.

openings.title: A desk turning chatbot-harm court records into evidence on lab safety
openings.summary: Chatbot-harm lawsuits produce filings, expert reports and testimony about how labs tested and shipped their models. Nobody reads these as safety evidence, and settlements can bury them. A small legal-research desk would collect, code and publish what the public record shows, and push for settlements and remedies that disclose more.
openings.detail: The Tech Justice Law Project (bridge) was counsel in Garcia v. Character Technologies, and in 2026 it filed Carrier and Lines v. OpenAI Foundation. In January 2026 Character.AI and Google agreed to settle five teen-harm suits, Garcia among them, which shows how quickly evidence can vanish into settlements. Trackers exist, such as TJLP's TRAL tracker with Knight-Georgetown and Georgetown CCT, but they count cases. They do not extract what the cases reveal about evaluations, red-teaming, known risks and decisions to ship. Others need that factual base: the ALI's Principles of the Law on civil liability for AI (adjacent), OII's 'careless speech' work, and safety researchers writing about lab practice. Success would be a public, coded record of the safety-relevant facts in every major AI-harm case, cited by AISIs, the ALI reporters and model-spec authors. It would also mean settlement terms that require disclosure and independent monitoring. The risks are real. Protective orders and sealed discovery limit what is public. The desk could look like plaintiff advocacy, so it needs a neutral host such as a law-school clinic, with input from defence lawyers. And most cases concern companion harms rather than catastrophic risk, although what they show about how labs decide to ship carries over.
steps: List the AI-harm dockets (the OpenAI and Character.AI suicide and psychosis suits, Social Media Victims Law Center cases, the FTC's 2025 orders to companion-chatbot makers) and code public filings against a template drawn from frontier safety frameworks.
Host the desk in a US law-school clinic, with advisers from TJLP and the defence bar and one safety researcher to frame the coding.
Where protective orders cover safety-relevant material, file public-interest motions to unseal, and draft model settlement terms with disclosure and independent-monitor clauses.
Publish a brief twice a year for AISIs, the ALI reporters and lab safety teams.
openings.evidence: Law x assurance has 34 entries, but only 4 of 93 law entries transfer into the model. TJLP is the only litigation organisation on the map. The sociotech angle notes list this as an unowned bridge ('litigation-to-safety translation desk'). Garcia was settled in January 2026.

openings.title: Human-rights due diligence for frontier AI, tested through investors
openings.summary: In September 2026 the UN human rights chief asked frontier AI companies for human-rights due diligence that includes agreed safety standards, incident reporting and independent monitoring. Nobody has yet written what that means for catastrophic risks. A joint team from business-and-human-rights and frontier-safety evaluation would write that protocol and pilot it, using investors and national human rights institutions to press for adoption.
openings.detail: The UN Guiding Principles already rank harms by scale, scope and irremediability, a test that fits catastrophic, irreversible risks better than most AI-ethics frameworks. They come with tools already in use: OHCHR B-Tech's foundation-model papers and its product workstream with BSR (adjacent), DIHR's guide to fundamental rights impact assessments and its NHRI Digital Rights Alliance (adjacent), the Council of Europe's HUDERIA method (adjacent), OECD National Contact Points, and engagement by faith-based investors through ICCR and the Investor Alliance for Human Rights (religion>law, adjacent). Frontier safety frameworks set capability thresholds and evaluations, but they offer no rights-based remedy and no external route for complaints. None of the 93 law entries connects the two sides. Success would be a published protocol that maps the elements of frontier safety frameworks onto the Guiding Principles' steps. It would be used in at least one investor engagement and one NHRI review, and cited by AISIs. There are three risks. Due diligence can turn into box-ticking. Rights groups such as Derechos Digitales and Fundación Vía Libre are sceptical of x-risk framing. And labs may welcome a soft standard as a way to avoid regulation, so the protocol has to keep the Guiding Principles' remedy and independent-monitoring elements.
steps: Bring B-Tech, DIHR and a frontier evaluator (an AISI or an independent evaluation group) together for a short drafting sprint on how the Guiding Principles' test of severity maps onto capability thresholds and incident reporting.
Pilot it with ICCR members and other responsible investors that hold shares in frontier-lab parent companies, as engagement asks for the 2027 AGM season.
Ask one national human rights institution, DIHR, to review a lab's published safety framework against the protocol.
Feed the results into the Council of Europe Convention's Conference of the Parties and the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.
openings.evidence: Türk's letter of September 2026 asks frontier AI companies for exactly this. B-Tech, DIHR, the Council of Europe and ICCR are all adjacent, and all transfer into institutions. Of 93 law profiles, 52 are framed around present harms and 2 around catastrophic risk. The sociotech angle notes list this as a bridge no organisation owns.

openings.title: A standing STS observatory studying how AI-safety knowledge is made
openings.summary: STS and anthropology have studied how physics, biomedicine and climate science produce knowledge, but no organisation does this for AI safety: its evaluations, forecasts, safety cases and stories about the future. A small observatory would place ethnographers and controversy mappers alongside safety organisations and report back to the field, a direct answer to the narrowing the brief describes.
openings.detail: The scholarly interest exists. At 4S's 2026 meeting, 26 of 244 open panels had AI in the title, and EASST 2026 had at least 13 AI panels. But 4S, EASST and CASTAC sit in the potential ring with no AI programme, and EPIC, whose members are ethnographers inside companies, only convenes. The blind-spot sweep found no organisation whose main work is ethnography of AI labs or of the safety community, no history of AI-risk ideas, and no AI programme at Mellon, Wenner-Gren or the SSRC. The nearest efforts have ended or are narrow. Shaping AI has been dormant since February 2024, though its French team had begun work on a safety meme. The Cambridge Histories of AI seminar has closed. IAS's SINAI studies narratives of AI. The Computer History Museum's new AI Archive preserves records rather than analysing them. Sciences Po's médialab in Paris and the Weizenbaum Institute in Berlin have the methods and sit near int/a hubs. Success would be two or three embedded researchers publishing studies of evaluation validity, forecasting practice and safety-case culture that safety organisations actually use, plus a map of AI-risk debates updated each year. The risks: much critical STS rejects the x-risk frame, safety organisations may refuse access or treat the work as PR, and results come slowly. The observatory needs a host that both sides trust and a brief that does not instrumentalise the research.
steps: Run a small call through 4S and EASST for STS and anthropology researchers to spend 6 to 12 months embedded with willing safety organisations: evaluators, AISIs and forecasting groups.
Commission médialab, or the former Shaping AI team, to map AI-risk controversies with its digital methods.
int/a hosts an annual meeting where the findings go back to safety practitioners.
Ask Mellon or Wenner-Gren to co-fund, since neither has an AI programme.
openings.evidence: Five of the 8 law entries in the potential ring are STS or history bodies. The blind-spot sweep marked ethnography of the safety community 'thin', the history of AI-risk ideas 'thin', and humanities funders 'searched_none_found'. 4S and EASST panel counts as above. Shaping AI is dormant and Histories of AI is closed.

openings.title: Apply Wales's future-generations law to public-sector AI adoption
openings.summary: Wales has a statutory guardian for people not yet born, and its 2023-30 strategy names AI as a theme running through all its missions, yet the office has published nothing on AI. Funding a Section 20-style review of how Welsh public bodies adopt AI, with AI-safety and futures expertise, would create the first statutory long-term impact test for AI and a template for other future-generations institutions.
openings.detail: The Future Generations Commissioner for Wales (potential, transfer none_yet) is the only organisation on the map that represents future generations in law. Law x systemic has just 3 entries: the Commissioner, LAVITS and LAPIN. Its Cymru Can strategy lists AI among the themes that connect its missions. Yet neither the 2025 Future Generations Report nor the 2025-26 annual report mentions AI, while the Welsh Government follows an AI plan led by growth. The Welsh Language Commissioner (adjacent) has already shown that a Welsh statutory office can extend its remit to AI without new legislation. The Centre for Future Generations in Brussels (bridge, on the classic map) has the AI-policy expertise to help. Success would be a published review or guidance that applies the Act's five ways of working (long term, prevention, integration, collaboration, involvement) to how public bodies buy and deploy AI. It would then be shared with similar bodies such as Hungary's deputy ombudsman for future generations and Finland's Committee for the Future. The risks: the office is small and its 2026 priorities are climate, energy and inequality. AI may be framed only as jobs and the productivity of public services. And the benefit for frontier safety is indirect. This builds a governance template; it does not reduce risk directly.
steps: int/a's London hub, or the Centre for Future Generations, opens a conversation with the Commissioner's office about AI as a Cymru Can cross-cutting theme, offering pro bono research support.
Fund a scoping paper on what the Act's well-being duty requires of Welsh public bodies that deploy AI agents and automated decision-making.
Pilot a futures workshop with one public body, for example an NHS Wales health board, using the Commissioner's existing futures tools.
Share the results with other future-generations institutions and with the follow-up to the UN Declaration on Future Generations.
openings.evidence: The Commissioner is potential with transfer none_yet, and no AI appears in its 2025 reports. Law x systemic has 3 entries. Cymru Can names AI as a cross-cutting theme. The Welsh Language Commissioner has a 2025 AI regulatory statement.

sector:peace.overview: The peace tradition brings the oldest tested toolkit for handling dangerous technology between rivals: arms control and verification, confidence-building measures and hotlines, Track II and scientist-to-scientist diplomacy, the humanitarian-law doctrine of meaningful human control, and mediation. Its main actors fall into three clusters. The first is Track II channels: safe-ai-forum, concordia-ai, oxford-martin-ai-governance-initiative, brookings-tsinghua-us-china-track-ii-dialogue-on and centre-for-humanitarian-dialogue. The second is arms-control institutes, mostly funded by carnegie-corporation-of-new-york: stockholm-international-peace-research-institute, european-leadership-network, institute-for-security-and-technology, pugwash-conferences-on-science-and-world-affairs and nuclear-threat-initiative. The third is humanitarian-law and UN bodies: international-committee-of-the-red-cross, stop-killer-robots and un-institute-for-disarmament-research. Peace sits fairly close to the AI-safety core: 28 of its 51 entries are core or bridge, and 6 are on the aisafety.com map. That closeness is almost entirely in diplomacy and arms control, and it reaches AI mostly through AI in nuclear command and military AI rather than frontier loss of control. Peacebuilding and mediation (11 entries) stay at adjacent and potential.
sector:peace.missing: Peacebuilding's own knowledge is not being applied to AI itself: conflict analysis, mediation, ripeness, de-escalation and dialogue across enemies. Of the 11 peacebuilding entries, none is core and only centre-for-humanitarian-dialogue is bridge. No peace organisation works on the race between labs or between the AI camps, or on conflict between AI agents. None of the 51 moves its knowledge into the model or to the builders.

cell_notes.note: Six entries. Five are diplomacy (safe-ai-forum, concordia-ai, oxford-martin-ai-governance-initiative, simon-institute-for-longterm-governance, ai-safety-asia), one is arms control (uchicago-existential-risk-laboratory) and none is peacebuilding. The thin arms-control count is partly a tagging choice: institute-for-security-and-technology was moved from core to bridge, yet its Recursive Self-Improvement Initiative is the only arms-control project aimed at frontier loss of control. The peacebuilding zero is a real opening. No AI-safety organisation is built on mediation or conflict transformation, and Search for Common Ground and Beyond Conflict, both on the starting list, showed no AI engagement.

Twenty-two entries: 12 arms control and 9 diplomacy, but only 1 peacebuilding. That one is centre-for-humanitarian-dialogue, whose state-to-state military-AI work is discreet and could not be verified after 2023. This is a real opening, not an artefact. The peacebuilders that do have AI programmes (cmi-martti-ahtisaari-peace-foundation, build-up, toda-peace-institute, un-dppa-innovation-cell) use AI in peace processes ('AI for peace'). They do not apply peace practice to AI risk, so they sit in adjacent.

Sixteen entries, of which only one is diplomacy (diplofoundation). This is mostly a definitional effect rather than an opening: diplomacy bodies that take up AI usually frame it as security or catastrophic risk, which puts them in bridge. It may also be partly a search artefact, because tech-diplomacy networks and foreign-ministry tech envoys were not swept systematically. Low priority.

Seven entries: four peacebuilding, two arms control (fest-forschungsst-tte-der-evangelischen-studieng, geneva-academy-of-international-humanitarian-law) and one diplomacy (geneva-science-and-diplomacy-anticipator). Search limits are the main reason the cell is thin. This angle's web-search budget ran out after about 27 queries, and the BICC and VDW sites could not be read. The bodies with the most transferable methods were noted in the discovery notes but not profiled: verification bodies (IAEA, CTBTO, OPCW, VERTIC), negotiation-science centres (Harvard PON, Stanford SCICN), conflict-data producers (Uppsala UCDP, ACLED), and Search for Common Ground. That these hold relevant methods but do no AI work is itself the opening, so a second pass should add to this cell.

sector:peace.key_insight: Of the 51 peace organisations, 45 (88%) have security as their primary problem. That is the narrowest focus of any tradition on the map; the next narrowest are indigenous (80%) and minds, safety and economics (77-79%). Peace is also the only tradition with four empty problem cells on the AI side: agency, values, ai_status and multi_agent. In 39 of 51 entries the knowledge goes into institutions, and in none does it go into the model or to the builders. So the field that studies conflict between agents for a living has no presence in multi-agent AI. Its AI work runs almost entirely through states, treaties and nuclear command and control.

openings.title: Professional mediators applying conflict transformation to the AI race
openings.summary: No one treats the frontier-lab race, or the hostility between the AI-safety, AI-ethics and accelerationist camps, as a conflict to analyse and mediate with peacebuilding methods. A small programme run by experienced mediators, starting with a conflict analysis and a camp-to-camp dialogue, would test whether those methods can lower the temperature where game-theoretic race models only describe it.
openings.detail: Peacebuilding's core tools (conflict analysis of actors, interests and positions; insider mediation; dialogue between parties who distrust each other) are absent from AI safety. The map shows this: there is no peacebuilding entry in core, and centre-for-humanitarian-dialogue is the only one in bridge, where it works on military AI between states. Berlin-based berghof-foundation holds these methods but has no AI work (transfer none_yet). cmi-martti-ahtisaari-peace-foundation has published AI principles for mediation, but it uses AI in peace processes rather than mediating AI's own conflicts. Industry forums coordinate the labs, but none is a mediated process, and int/a's principle of not making the race worse has no institutional home. Success in the first 18 months would be a published conflict analysis of the AI race written by mediators, plus at least one recurring, facilitated safety-ethics dialogue whose participants report better working relations. Risks: anything between labs needs antitrust counsel and must stick to safety topics. The conflict may not be ripe. Confidentiality also makes impact hard to show, which is the same problem safe-ai-forum and centre-for-humanitarian-dialogue already have.
steps: Commission berghof-foundation or cmi-martti-ahtisaari-peace-foundation to write a standard peacebuilding conflict analysis of the AI race (parties, interests, escalation dynamics, possible entry points), costed at a few months of mediator time.

int/a pilots a facilitated dialogue in Berlin or London between AI-ethics and AI-safety researchers, which carries lower stakes than working with the labs, and uses intelligence-rising's role-play to surface each side's assumptions.
Get antitrust advice and sound out lab policy and safety staff on a discreet Track 1.5 limited to safety topics such as incident sharing and red lines.
Have an outside peace researcher run a before-and-after evaluation, so the pilot's results can be read by funders outside the peace field.
openings.evidence: Peacebuilding is 11 of 51 peace entries, with 0 core and 1 bridge. berghof-foundation is the only peace entry tagged none_yet. The discovery notes, gap (a), found no one applying conflict transformation to the race between labs or between camps. Search for Common Ground and Beyond Conflict were checked and showed no AI engagement. A quick search for 2026 returned only work that uses AI in mediation (CSIS, CMI, Belfer), not mediation applied to AI.

openings.title: Fellowship bringing treaty-verification inspectors into AI-agreement verification work
openings.summary: Proposals for international AI agreements depend on verification, yet the people who have actually run inspection regimes (IAEA, CTBTO, OPCW, VERTIC) are not on the map. A placement fellowship modelled on IST's AI–Nuclear Policy Accelerator, plus bridge funding for the one interdisciplinary verification group already on the map, would move that practical knowledge across.
openings.detail: Arms-control verification has decades of practical experience that AI-agreement design needs: declarations, managed access, challenge inspections, and building technical bodies that rival states both trust. On the map, the verification work sits with researchers. prif-emerging-disruptive-technologies-research-g (CNTR) combines physicists, computer scientists and political scientists, but its funding period ends in December 2026 with no renewal confirmed. ifsh-institute-for-peace-research-and-security-p has a 2026 paper on AI assurance for the OPCW, and oxford-martin-ai-governance-initiative has published on verification for international AI governance. institute-for-security-and-technology's accelerator, funded by carnegie-corporation-of-new-york, already gave 26 nuclear practitioners AI literacy, which shows the placement model works. Success would be a cohort of 10-15 former inspectors and verification scientists placed in AI governance organisations and national AI safety institutes, producing joint designs for compute and model-verification regimes. Risks: technical work on compute verification already exists inside AI governance, so the fellowship should bring regime-design and inspection know-how rather than duplicate hardware research. Former inspectors may also be bound by confidentiality.
steps: Approach CNTR before December 2026 about bridge funding that keeps its verification group alive while a fellowship is designed.

Recruit a first cohort through VERTIC, CTBTO and OPCW alumni networks and the PRIF and IFSH arms-control networks, and place fellows with oxford-martin-ai-governance-initiative, institute-for-security-and-technology or national AI safety institutes.

Ask each fellow for a short design paper on one verifiable AI commitment (for example a compute threshold or a model-evaluation obligation), tested in a tabletop exercise with stanford-center-for-international-security-and-c or un-institute-for-disarmament-research.
openings.evidence: No verification body (IAEA, CTBTO, OPCW, VERTIC) is on the map, and gap (b) in the discovery notes says this expertise has barely reached compute governance. prif-emerging-disruptive-technologies-research-g's funding ends in December 2026. institute-for-security-and-technology's accelerator (26 fellows) is the model to copy. A quick search found academic papers on lessons from nuclear verification for AI treaties and a CTBTO fellowship limited to nuclear work, but no AI verification placement scheme.

openings.title: Mediators and negotiation scholars co-building evaluations for AI-agent conflict
openings.summary: The peace x multi_agent cell is empty, even though conflict between agents is the peace field's core subject and AI agents are starting to bargain and escalate against each other. A research programme pairing professional mediators and negotiation scholars with cooperative-AI researchers would turn concepts such as ripeness, face-saving and third-party mediation into tests of how AI agents escalate and settle conflicts.
openings.detail: Multi-agent AI is the least-covered problem on the whole map (34 entries, 14 primary), and the discovery notes say peace-and-conflict researchers and mediators are absent from AI–AI conflict, with CLR almost alone. Cooperative-AI groups on the map (foundations-of-cooperative-ai-lab, witt-lab-university-of-oxford-moving-to-ucl, modeling-cooperation, equilibria-network) and the Concordia simulation library work mostly from game theory and computer science. Practitioner knowledge sits in geneva-centre-for-security-policy (its PIN negotiation programme, not yet applied to AI), cmi-martti-ahtisaari-peace-foundation and centre-for-humanitarian-dialogue. The democracy notes add a second gap: no one systematically red-teams AI mediators (habermas-machine is dormant). Success would be an open evaluation suite that tests whether LLM agents recognise deadlock, take face-saving exits, accept a mediator's single negotiating text, or escalate, developed by mixed teams of mediators and researchers. Risks: mediators' skill is largely tacit and may not translate. Better negotiating agents are also a capability, so evaluations should measure escalation and failure to settle rather than train agents to win.
steps: Run a two-day workshop pairing PIN, CMI and HD practitioners with researchers from FOCAL, Witt Lab and the Concordia team to choose five concepts from mediation practice that can be tested in agents.
Fund three or four mediator–researcher pairs to build scenarios in the Concordia library, published as an open evaluation suite.

Approach multi-agent funders (macroscopic-ventures, schmidt-sciences, and the Cooperative AI Foundation, which is not on the map) to co-fund, and use findings on AI escalation in wargames as a second test bed.
openings.evidence: peace x multi_agent is one of four empty peace problem cells. multi_agent has 34 entries in total (14 primary), the fewest of any problem. None of the 51 peace entries transfers knowledge into the model. The neuro angle notes say mediation and diplomacy practitioners are absent from AI–AI conflict. geneva-centre-for-security-policy's profile says the link from PIN to AI agreements is a possibility, not current work.

openings.title: AI-risk modules in African peacekeeping and mediation training, co-designed with African practitioners
openings.summary: Africa has three home peace entries, Latin America and MENA none, and the two African peace-practice institutions on the map teach only how to use AI tools. A co-designed module on governing AI risk, delivered through the UCT hub and taught at KAIPTC and ACCORD, would build that capacity and bring African mediation practice into global AI governance.
openings.detail: kofi-annan-international-peacekeeping-training-c is one of the three ECOWAS training centres of excellence, but its AI courses teach the use of AI tools, not the governance of AI risk. african-centre-for-the-constructive-resolution-o has published two 2026 analysis pieces on AI and no programme. african-hub-on-ai-safety-peace-and-security at UCT, funded by IDRC and FCDO through idrc-artificial-intelligence-for-development, already runs an AI-diplomacy curriculum for African policymakers. It is the obvious partner to carry that curriculum into the training institutions that serve the AU and regional bodies. ilina-program and global-center-on-ai-governance add catastrophic-risk and inequality perspectives. Success would be a module taught at KAIPTC and ACCORD within a year, plus African mediators taking part in UN AI processes alongside simon-institute-for-longterm-governance. Risks: AU demand may centre on surveillance, drones and present harms. The module must be co-designed rather than import a Northern x-risk framing, or it will not be taken up.
steps: Fund a scoping meeting of african-hub-on-ai-safety-peace-and-security, KAIPTC and ACCORD to agree which AI-risk topics African peace-support practitioners actually need.
Pilot one short course at KAIPTC that pairs AI-risk content with African mediation case studies, taught jointly by the hub and ACCORD.
Link graduates to UN AI-governance processes through simon-institute-for-longterm-governance, and to Latin American counterparts through observatorio-de-riesgos-catastr-ficos-globales.
openings.evidence: Home peace entries by region: Africa 3 (two at potential), Latin America 0, MENA 0. 46 of 51 entries take neither a Majority-World nor an Indigenous-led standpoint. The profiles say KAIPTC's AI courses teach 'people to use AI tools, not to govern AI risks', and that ACCORD has no AI staff or programme. Gap (f) in the discovery notes says Africa and Latin America are almost absent.
